July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. PODCAST SERIES Ideas Listen as members of the research community at Microsoft discuss the beliefs that animate their research, the experiences and thinkers that inform it, and the positive human impact it targets. Listen now Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. items.content: Back to Articles How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications Team Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 28 +22 Bernardo França de Aguiar bernardoaguiar Follow Dharma-AI Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves falves9101 Follow Dharma-AI Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications. In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model. The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step. One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency. The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses. We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication. A Vocabulary Built for Everyone The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense. For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once. The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request. The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses. Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill. To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill , the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode , the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth. This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading. Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings. The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model. And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows. Why Existing Solutions Fell Short Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations. They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve. They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one. How We Solved It VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first. First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly. Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget. To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points. Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain. An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated. A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running. That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%. What Changed in the Grader To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime. The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810. Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version. The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter. Beyond the Grader To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling. VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803. Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe. Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary. The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.32926 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026] Title: ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators Authors: Aaditya Prasad , Steven W. Flavell , Brian DePasquale View a PDF of the paper titled ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators, by Aaditya Prasad and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory. ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators Aaditya Prasad Affiliation: Picower Institute for Learning & Memory Affiliation: Department of Brain & Cognitive Sciences Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Email: aaprasad@mit.edu Steven W. Flavell Affiliation: Howard Hughes Medical Institute Affiliation: Picower Institute for Learning & Memory Affiliation: Department of Brain & Cognitive Sciences Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Email: flavell@mit.edu Brian DePasquale Affiliation: Department of Biomedical Engineering Affiliation: Boston University Affiliation: Boston, MA 02215, USA Email: bddepasq@bu.edu Abstract State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Z akai E quation N eural O perator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO’s ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized C. elegans nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory. 1 Introduction Estimating a latent dynamical process from a set of noisy observations is a fundamental problem in machine learning for science ( Durstewitz et al., 2023 ) . For example, in neuroscience, it is thought that neural computations are implemented by a latent dynamical system that is expressed by a neural population ( Saxena and Cunningham, 2019 ) . This problem has been well studied in signal-processing as filtering (in the online setting) or smoothing (in the offline setting) a noisy non-linear dynamical system ( Yau et al., 2024 ) . The essence of filtering as Bayesian inference is to estimate the filtering distribution p ( 𝐳 t | X [ 0 : t ] ) p(\mathbf{z}_{t}|X_{[{0:t}]}) where 𝐳 t ∈ ℝ n \mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is an unobserved latent variable and 𝐱 t ∈ ℝ m \mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} ( m ≥ n m\geq n ) are observations at each point t ∈ [ 0 , T ] t\in[0,T] , while for smoothing the goal is to estimate the posterior distribution p ( 𝐳 t | X [ 0 : T ] ) p(\mathbf{z}_{t}|X_{[0:T]}) ( Sarkka, 2013 ) . These distributions are referred to as the filtering and smoothing distributions respectively. For continuous time systems, the dynamics of the filtering distribution has been well studied as the Kushner-Stratonovich (KS) equation ( Stratonovich, 1960 ; Kushner, 1964 ) , a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE). A more tractable analog of the KS equation is the Zakai equation ( Zakai, 1969 ) , a linear SPDE governing the unnormalized posterior density. While solving the KS or Zakai equation provides the exact posterior distribution (post-normalization for the Zakai equation), solving these equations is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically for high-dimensional systems ( Sabbar and Nisar, 2025 ) . Alternative methods such as state-space models ( Bishop, 2006 ) , (switching) linear dynamical systems ( Linderman et al., 2017 ) , and deep learning-based latent stochastic differential equations (SDE) ( Li et al., 2020 ) offer a more tractable approach to inference and parameter learning by making assumptions or approximations about the posterior distribution. For example, the Kalman-Bucy filter ( Kalman and Bucy, 1961 ) provides the exact solution to the KS equation under the assumption that dynamics are linear and observation noise is Gaussian. Thus, the need remains for powerful methods that can approximate the filtering posterior without restrictive assumptions while remaining computationally tractable. Two recent approaches for solving PDEs with neural networks offer a route around these barriers. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) supervise the fit with the governing equation rather than labeled solutions, constraining the network’s autodifferentiated derivatives to satisfy the equation at a set of collocation points ( Raissi et al., 2019 ; Karniadakis et al., 2021 ) . PINNS are applicable when the solution is never observed, as in filtering, and because no parametric form is imposed, they can represent non-Gaussian posteriors governing nonlinear dynamics. However, PINNs are fit to a single instance of a PDE and must be retrained for each new one, whereas in filtering every observation path X [ 0 , t ] X_{[0,t]} drives a distinct instance of the Zakai equation. Neural operators learn the solution operator itself, mapping a PDE’s defining data to its solution and generalizing across instances without retraining ( Lu et al., 2021 ; Azizzadenesheli et al., 2024 ) , but are trained on labeled solutions which filtering never provides. Physics-informed neural operators (PINOs) resolve both obstacles, using the equation’s residual when observations are unavailable to supervise operator learning across a distribution of instances ( Wang et al., 2021b ; Li et al., 2024 ) . This is the paradigm we build on to solve the Zakai equation for nonlinear filtering. We present the Z akai E quation N eural O perator (ZENO): A physics-informed neural operator for nonlinear filtering that learns the solution to the Zakai equation. ZENO represents the unnormalized filtering distribution by optimizing a physics informed loss which minimizes the residual between the PINO’s posterior derivatives and the Fokker Planck operator while incorporating likelihood updates at observation times. Unlike current approaches, which use numerical solvers ( Leng et al., 2026 ) for forecasting or a deep-splitting approach ( Beck et al., 2021 ; Bågmark et al., 2023b ; Bågmark et al., 2023a ; Beck et al., 2026 ) , we leverage neural operators to learn a global solution over the entire observation history. Furthermore, we make no assumptions about the form of the dynamics model and instead estimate the dynamical parameters and observation model in an expectation-maximization ( Dempster et al., 1977 ) like setup. We show that ZENO is able to achieve similar latent inference accuracy to optimal nonlinear filters in simulated dynamical systems. We then show that ZENO performs dynamical parameter estimation at the same level as other state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines. Finally, we evaluate our model on a real world neuroscience dataset and find that ZENO is able to recapitulate previously observed latent dynamical structure. 2 Methods 2.1 Background 2.1.1 Problem Formulation The problem of nonlinear filtering involves estimating the posterior distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐳 t ∣ X [ 0 , t ] ) p(\mathbf{z}_{t}\mid X_{[0,t]}) , where 𝐳 t ∈ ℝ n \mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is an unobserved latent state and X [ 0 , t ] = { 𝐱 t k : t k ≤ t } X_{[0,t]}=\{\mathbf{x}_{t_{k}}:t_{k}\leq t\} are noisy m m -dimensional observations of 𝐳 \mathbf{z} taken at discrete times t k = k ​ Δ ​ t t_{k}=k\Delta t . Differential equations are naturally expressed in terms of operators: the equation itself defines one operator acting on the unknown function, and its solution — when it exists — defines another, the operator that maps the equation’s data to that solution. For example, for the Fokker-Planck equation, the operator of interest is 𝒢 : p 0 ↦ p ⁡ ( ⋅ , t ) \mathcal{G}:p_{0}\mapsto p(\cdot,t) , mapping an initial density to the solution at later times. Neural operators are the generalization of neural networks from functions between finite dimensional vector spaces to infinite dimensional functional spaces (Appendix A ). They are commonly used to learn the solution operators to differential equations, especially PDEs. We evaluate our model on its latent and dynamical RMSE as well as its ability to reconstruct observations 3.1.1 Latent Inference We first tested how well ZENO could infer the filtering posterior for a double well potential. This system is used in neuroscience as a simple model of decision making and is of interest because the posterior distribution can be bimodal ( Duncker et al., 2019 ) . Because the state is low dimensional and we have access to the exact drift and diffusion, it is tractable to numerically solve the Zakai equation to access the Bayes optimal filter for comparison. In general, this would not be possible as numerical solvers scale exponentially with the dimension of the PDE they are solving. Fig 2 A shows that we are able to represent the exact filtering distribution and its mean estimate while Fig 2 B and C show that our model is able to scale to a higher dimensional system and accurately reconstruct the VDP oscillator and Lorenz system. We find that ZENO reaches the ceiling set by the optimal filter for the double well equation and Van Der Pol oscillator but gaps the optimal filter by about 0.005 0.005 on the Lorenz system Lorenz (1963) (Fig. 2 D). B) Latent Posterior Mean Estimate for the Van Der Pol System. C) Latent Trajectory Inference for the Lorenz Attractor. D) Comparison of ZENO’s normalized root mean squared error with the exact optimal filter for each system. 3.1.2 Dynamics Parameter Learning After we validated that latent inference by ZENO was accurate, we asked how well it learns system parameters. Fig 3 A shows that ZENO learns the double well potential’s cubic drift. On Van Der Pol, we show that ZENO reproduces the limit cycle but the velocity field is slower at the edges of the domain (Fig 3 B). Finally, on Lorenz we find that ZENO reconstructs the dynamics but misestimates some directions and speeds of the flow field (Fig 3 C). ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators Aaditya Prasad Affiliation: Picower Institute for Learning & Memory Affiliation: Department of Brain & Cognitive Sciences Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Email: aaprasad@mit.edu Steven W. Flavell Affiliation: Howard Hughes Medical Institute Affiliation: Picower Institute for Learning & Memory Affiliation: Department of Brain & Cognitive Sciences Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Email: flavell@mit.edu Brian DePasquale Affiliation: Department of Biomedical Engineering Affiliation: Boston University Affiliation: Boston, MA 02215, USA Email: bddepasq@bu.edu Abstract State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Z akai E quation N eural O perator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO’s ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized C. elegans nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory. 1 Introduction Estimating a latent dynamical process from a set of noisy observations is a fundamental problem in machine learning for science ( Durstewitz et al., 2023 ) . For example, in neuroscience, it is thought that neural computations are implemented by a latent dynamical system that is expressed by a neural population ( Saxena and Cunningham, 2019 ) . This problem has been well studied in signal-processing as filtering (in the online setting) or smoothing (in the offline setting) a noisy non-linear dynamical system ( Yau et al., 2024 ) . The essence of filtering as Bayesian inference is to estimate the filtering distribution p ( 𝐳 t | X [ 0 : t ] ) p(\mathbf{z}_{t}|X_{[{0:t}]}) where 𝐳 t ∈ ℝ n \mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is an unobserved latent variable and 𝐱 t ∈ ℝ m \mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} ( m ≥ n m\geq n ) are observations at each point t ∈ [ 0 , T ] t\in[0,T] , while for smoothing the goal is to estimate the posterior distribution p ( 𝐳 t | X [ 0 : T ] ) p(\mathbf{z}_{t}|X_{[0:T]}) ( Sarkka, 2013 ) . These distributions are referred to as the filtering and smoothing distributions respectively. For continuous time systems, the dynamics of the filtering distribution has been well studied as the Kushner-Stratonovich (KS) equation ( Stratonovich, 1960 ; Kushner, 1964 ) , a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE). A more tractable analog of the KS equation is the Zakai equation ( Zakai, 1969 ) , a linear SPDE governing the unnormalized posterior density. While solving the KS or Zakai equation provides the exact posterior distribution (post-normalization for the Zakai equation), solving these equations is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically for high-dimensional systems ( Sabbar and Nisar, 2025 ) . Alternative methods such as state-space models ( Bishop, 2006 ) , (switching) linear dynamical systems ( Linderman et al., 2017 ) , and deep learning-based latent stochastic differential equations (SDE) ( Li et al., 2020 ) offer a more tractable approach to inference and parameter learning by making assumptions or approximations about the posterior distribution. For example, the Kalman-Bucy filter ( Kalman and Bucy, 1961 ) provides the exact solution to the KS equation under the assumption that dynamics are linear and observation noise is Gaussian. Thus, the need remains for powerful methods that can approximate the filtering posterior without restrictive assumptions while remaining computationally tractable. Two recent approaches for solving PDEs with neural networks offer a route around these barriers. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) supervise the fit with the governing equation rather than labeled solutions, constraining the network’s autodifferentiated derivatives to satisfy the equation at a set of collocation points ( Raissi et al., 2019 ; Karniadakis et al., 2021 ) . PINNS are applicable when the solution is never observed, as in filtering, and because no parametric form is imposed, they can represent non-Gaussian posteriors governing nonlinear dynamics. However, PINNs are fit to a single instance of a PDE and must be retrained for each new one, whereas in filtering every observation path X [ 0 , t ] X_{[0,t]} drives a distinct instance of the Zakai equation. Neural operators learn the solution operator itself, mapping a PDE’s defining data to its solution and generalizing across instances without retraining ( Lu et al., 2021 ; Azizzadenesheli et al., 2024 ) , but are trained on labeled solutions which filtering never provides. Physics-informed neural operators (PINOs) resolve both obstacles, using the equation’s residual when observations are unavailable to supervise operator learning across a distribution of instances ( Wang et al., 2021b ; Li et al., 2024 ) . This is the paradigm we build on to solve the Zakai equation for nonlinear filtering. We present the Z akai E quation N eural O perator (ZENO): A physics-informed neural operator for nonlinear filtering that learns the solution to the Zakai equation. ZENO represents the unnormalized filtering distribution by optimizing a physics informed loss which minimizes the residual between the PINO’s posterior derivatives and the Fokker Planck operator while incorporating likelihood updates at observation times. Unlike current approaches, which use numerical solvers ( Leng et al., 2026 ) for forecasting or a deep-splitting approach ( Beck et al., 2021 ; Bågmark et al., 2023b ; Bågmark et al., 2023a ; Beck et al., 2026 ) , we leverage neural operators to learn a global solution over the entire observation history. Furthermore, we make no assumptions about the form of the dynamics model and instead estimate the dynamical parameters and observation model in an expectation-maximization ( Dempster et al., 1977 ) like setup. We show that ZENO is able to achieve similar latent inference accuracy to optimal nonlinear filters in simulated dynamical systems. We then show that ZENO performs dynamical parameter estimation at the same level as other state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines. Finally, we evaluate our model on a real world neuroscience dataset and find that ZENO is able to recapitulate previously observed latent dynamical structure. 2 Methods 2.1 Background 2.1.1 Problem Formulation The problem of nonlinear filtering involves estimating the posterior distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐳 t ∣ X [ 0 , t ] ) p(\mathbf{z}_{t}\mid X_{[0,t]}) , where 𝐳 t ∈ ℝ n \mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is an unobserved latent state and X [ 0 , t ] = { 𝐱 t k : t k ≤ t } X_{[0,t]}=\{\mathbf{x}_{t_{k}}:t_{k}\leq t\} are noisy m m -dimensional observations of 𝐳 \mathbf{z} taken at discrete times t k = k ​ Δ ​ t t_{k}=k\Delta t . Differential equations are naturally expressed in terms of operators: the equation itself defines one operator acting on the unknown function, and its solution — when it exists — defines another, the operator that maps the equation’s data to that solution. items.title: Agent Lightning v1.0: A 3,500-Line Lightweight Agentic RL Framework for Training Agents with Real Harnesses

items.content: At a glance Harnessed Agentic RL: Microsoft Research Asia introduces a training paradigm in which the same agent harness used in deployment participates directly in reinforcement learning, removing the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. Lightweight by design: Agent Lightning v1.0 delivers a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code. Native Kubernetes support: agents run as standard Kubernetes jobs on self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, with no dependency on paid commercial sandbox services. Data-efficient training recipe: an end-to-end coding agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage point gain, using only about 6,000 training samples based on open sourced dataset. AI agents have evolved from single models to complex full-stack systems built from models, tools, and execution environments. Their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an approach where AI systems learn through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for their actions. RL can make those agents better, but most agent RL systems require developers to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. That is costly, and it means the agent being trained is not quite the agent that gets deployed. To address this, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia have introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open-sourced a fully rebuilt Agent Lightning v1.0 (opens in new tab) . Compared with the original, Agent Lightning, v1.0 puts more emphasis on staying lightweight, on integrating with real harnesses, and on a complete, reproducible agent RL training pipeline. Agent Lightning v1.0 was rebuilt around Harnessed Agentic RL, with key improvements: Lightweight : the entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code. Agent Lightning v1.0 implements a complete Harnessed Agentic RL system in a codebase that is small and clear enough to understand, modify, and extend. Training on a real agent harness : agents reach the model through the large language model (LLM) proxy in Agent Lightning v1.0, leaving existing harness code unchanged. Native Kubernetes support : agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, without external commercial sandbox services. Self-managed clusters and local infrastructure alike can support rollouts at scale. A complete coding agent training example : an end-to-end pipeline built on Qwen3.5-9B raised Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, an absolute gain of 14.6 percentage points, using only about 6,000 training samples. The limits of traditional agentic RL Traditional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop with the environment. In a ReAct-style loop, the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, the observation is appended to the context, and the model generates the next action, so the whole rollout maps onto one continuous token trajectory. Early RL systems such as verl, AReaL, and slime were built this way, which meant training an agent required rebuilding its loop inside the RL framework. Real harnesses have outgrown that assumption. Coding agents such as mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex each bring their own context management, tool protocols, execution logic, and dependencies, as do general-purpose agent systems. Rebuilding one for training is expensive, and the rebuilt agent may no longer behave in the same way as the deployed agent. Agent Lightning takes a different route. It places an LLM proxy between the agent and the model. The agent continues to run as before: simply point the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, and the training framework can observe and record its model calls. In v1.0, the researchers go further and formally define this paradigm as Harnessed Agentic RL: whichever agent harness is used in deployment is the harness that takes part directly in reinforcement learning during training (Figure 1). Figure 1. Traditional agentic RL compared with Harnessed Agentic RL. In traditional agentic RL, the training framework manages the environment and the agent loop. In Harnessed Agentic RL, the harness manages both. Four challenges in training with real harnesses A core difference between Harnessed Agentic RL and traditional agentic RL is that the environment interaction loop is handled by the agent harness rather than the training framework. The training system can only observe a series of LLM request and response pairs, so a single rollout may be split into a variable number of training samples. This brings four key challenges: Retokenization and sample merging : Harnesses keep context as text, but RL training needs the token IDs sampled during the rollout. Passing text through the chat template and tokenizer again can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls cannot always be merged into one sample. Advantage calculation : Retokenization, subagents and context summarization can split one rollout into several samples. Computing baselines and advantages directly at the sample level causes rollouts that produce more samples to be counted repeatedly, which alters the original statistical relationships at the rollout level. Loss normalization : Averaging loss by sample count gives more weight to rollouts that produce more samples. Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it. Training backend scheduling : Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2). The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training. Figure 2. The Agent Lightning v1.0 system architecture showing the API gateway, rollout controller, and customized trainer. Collocated async RL Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs. Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3). Figure 3. Synchronous RL, asynchronous RL, and Collocated Async RL compared. Collocated Async RL raises utilization while occupying fewer GPUs. Running agents on Kubernetes Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible. Figure 4. The Rollout Controller in Agent Lightning v1.0 provides native Kubernetes support, running agents directly as standard Kubernetes jobs. 6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points. The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5). Figure 5. Pass rate and policy entropy for Qwen3.5-9B on the SWE-smith validation set. This brings four key challenges: Retokenization and sample merging : Harnesses keep context as text, but RL training needs the token IDs sampled during the rollout. Passing text through the chat template and tokenizer again can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls cannot always be merged into one sample. Advantage calculation : Retokenization, subagents and context summarization can split one rollout into several samples. Computing baselines and advantages directly at the sample level causes rollouts that produce more samples to be counted repeatedly, which alters the original statistical relationships at the rollout level. Loss normalization : Averaging loss by sample count gives more weight to rollouts that produce more samples. Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it. Training backend scheduling : Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2). The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training. Figure 2. The Agent Lightning v1.0 system architecture showing the API gateway, rollout controller, and customized trainer. Collocated async RL Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs. Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3). Figure 3. Synchronous RL, asynchronous RL, and Collocated Async RL compared. Collocated Async RL raises utilization while occupying fewer GPUs. Running agents on Kubernetes Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible. Figure 4. The Rollout Controller in Agent Lightning v1.0 provides native Kubernetes support, running agents directly as standard Kubernetes jobs. 6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points. The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5). Figure 5. Pass rate and policy entropy for Qwen3.5-9B on the SWE-smith validation set. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. ACADEMIC CONFERENCE Microsoft at SOSP 2026 Academic and industrial participants present research and experience papers that cover the full range of theory and practice of computer systems software. Learn more Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) .
