items.content: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms Xi Chen 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU Fengqi Hu 1 1 footnotemark: 1 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU Zeyu Shen 1 1 footnotemark: 1 3 3 footnotemark: 3 Affiliation: JHU Jiaying Xu 5 5 footnotemark: 5 Affiliation: UCSD Shangding Gu 6 6 footnotemark: 6 Affiliation: UC Berkeley Pan Xu 7 7 footnotemark: 7 Affiliation: Duke Anqi Liu 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU Laixi Shi 4 4 footnotemark: 4 Affiliation: JHU October 23, 2026 Abstract Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib , an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms. The code and tutorial are available at https://robustrl-lib.github.io . Keywords: Robust RL, benchmark, algorithm library, distribution shift, sim-to-real transfer Figure 1 : The overview of RobustRLlib . 1 Introduction Despite remarkable advances in reinforcement learning (RL), its real-world deployment remains limited by robustness and safety concerns, particularly in high-stakes domains such as autonomous driving ( Ding et al., 2023b ) , clinical trials ( Liu et al., 2015 ) , robotics ( Li et al., 2021 ) , and semiconductor manufacturing ( Kozak et al., 2023 ) . Policies trained in idealized environments can easily fail under distribution shifts or disruptions affecting various stages of the interaction, such as observations ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Han et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2021 ; Xiong et al., 2022 ) , actions ( Huang et al., 2017 ) , or environment dynamics ( Iyengar, 2005 ; Pinto et al., 2017 ) , induced by diverse factors such as sim-to-real gaps ( Pinto et al., 2017 ) , model uncertainty ( Bertsimas et al., 2019 ) , noise, or adversarial attacks ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Klopp et al., 2017 ; Mahmood et al., 2018 ) . Robust RL therefore aims to develop policies that remain reliable under diverse types of disruptions and shifts, or their combinations in real-world scenarios ( Bertsimas et al., 2019 ; Tversky and Kahneman, 1974 ; Arthur, 1991 ) . A broad range of robust RL algorithms has shown strong performance in their specific type of disrupted application scenarios. More importantly, existing methods provide a rich set of robustness mechanisms and principles, including adversarial training ( Pinto et al., 2017 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Rigter et al., 2022 ) , dynamics randomization ( Peng et al., 2018 ) , robust value updates ( Yang et al., 2022 ; Panaganti et al., 2022 ) , and data augmentation ( Yu et al., 2020b ; Lu et al., 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ) , offering substantial promise across a far broader range of applications and shift scenarios. However, realizing this broader potential faces two fundamental barriers: algorithm reusability and systematic characterization of the capability boundary . First, existing robust RL algorithms are fragmented across separate implementations and training pipelines, lacking a unified library or interface through which practitioners can readily try and compare a broad collection of robust RL methods on a new application. Second, the empirical capability boundary of current robust RL remains unclear: for a given application and distribution shift, we lack a systematic understanding of how well existing methods perform, when they remain effective, and where they fail. This is largely because the methods are typically evaluated in distinct environments and shift scenarios, making cross-method comparison difficult and performance beyond their original settings poorly understood. To address these two gaps, we introduce RobustRLlib , an algorithm-centric robust RL benchmark that brings together (1) a robust RL method library with reusable implementations to substantially lower the barrier to applying existing methods to new problems, and (2) a comprehensive evaluation pipeline across tasks and diverse real-world shift scenarios. Complementing existing robust RL benchmarks that primarily focus on developing evaluation tasks and shift scenarios ( Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020 ; Zouitine et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) , RobustRLlib focuses on making robust RL algorithms systematically accessible, comparable, and extensible, while providing a broader evaluation framework (Comparison in Appendix A.1 ). Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • A robust RL algorithm library. We integrate existing 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms, understanding and systematically organizing them by their learning methods, intended target shifts, and base algorithms for applicators’ easy reference. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms. • An enhanced evaluation platform. Our extensible disruptor toolbox covers a broad range of distribution shifts, including MDP-element shifts in observations, actions, dynamics, and reward/cost, as well as control-loop latency and task-semantic shifts. It supports diverse shift modes, including stochastic, adversarial, and parametric perturbations with non-stationary schedules, enabling both isolated and compound-shift evaluation. The same disruptor interface further extends to massively parallel training in Isaac Lab ( Mittal et al., 2025 ) and advanced vision–language–action (VLA) robotic tasks ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . • An up-to-date capability map of robust RL algorithms. Evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations reveals that robust methods outperform standard references on average, but both groups deteriorate markedly as shifts intensify. A method’s claimed target shift does not reliably predict its empirical strengths, gains vary across tasks and shift sources, with online methods showing larger incremental effects than offline ones. By connecting diverse algorithm features to their measured strengths, this map provides guidance for designing robust RL methods for deployment shifts. 2 Related Work Robust RL problems under diverse deployment shifts. Robust RL addresses deployment shifts affecting different components and stages of the agent–environment interaction, and prior work can be categorized accordingly. Zhang et al. (2020) ; Zhang et al. (2021) ; Oikarinen et al. (2021) address observation shift , which perturbs policy inputs through sensing errors or external attacks. Tessler et al. (2019) ; Tan et al. (2020) address action shift , which perturbs or replaces executed actions. Dynamics shift , involving uncertainty in or changes to the transition kernel, is addressed either by optimizing worst-case performance over ambiguity sets ( Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005 ; Iyengar, 2005 ; Xu and Mannor, 2010 ; Wiesemann et al., 2013 ; Goyal and Grand-Clement, 2023 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Shi and Chi, 2024 ) or by introducing random or adversarial perturbations to physical parameters and external forces ( Rajeswaran et al., 2016 ; Peng et al., 2018 ; Pinto et al., 2017 ; Mankowitz et al., 2019 ) . Queeney and Benosman (2023) ; Ma et al. (2019) address reward and cost shifts through constraint-aware learning, and reward-poisoning analysis. Beyond these MDP components, Bouteiller et al. (2021) ; Peng et al. (2018) ; Tan et al. (2018) address latency shift , involving delays or irregularities in observation and action timing. Tobin et al. (2017) ; Ding et al. (2023a) address semantic shift , involving changes in appearance or task-relevant relationships among visual cues, objects, and goals. In practice, real-world scenarios may involve multiple shifts, such as changes in dynamics parameters, process noise, and observation noise ( Mandlekar et al., 2017 ) , or non-stationary shifts that evolve during deployment ( Lecarpentier and Rachelson, 2019 ) . Since robustness to one shift does not necessarily extend to others or their combinations, this motivates developing algorithms for co-occurring shifts and evaluating them under a unified framework. Robust RL algorithm taxonomy. Robust RL algorithms promote robustness through two main approaches: modifying the learning objective or algorithm ( learner-centric ) and modifying the training data distribution ( data-centric ). For robust online RL , learner-centric methods seek robust policies through optimization against an adversary ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) , worst-case robust value objectives ( Liang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2024 ) , smoothing the policy over perturbed observations ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , or causal-inspired data augmentation to handle spurious correlated shifted scenarios ( Ding et al., 2023a ) . Data-centric methods can collect trajectories by interacting with shifted environments through physical parameter randomization ( Peng et al., 2018 ) , model ensembles ( Rajeswaran et al., 2016 ; Mankowitz et al., 2019 ; Tanabe et al., 2022 ) , or by applying adversarial disturbances ( Pinto et al., 2017 ) . For robust offline RL , learner-centric methods address model uncertainty and limited data coverage through robust Bellman updates over an uncertainty set of transitions ( Panaganti et al., 2022 ; Blanchet et al., 2023 ; Panaganti et al., 2023 ) , and mitigate value overestimation by smoothness regularization over perturbed states ( Yang et al., 2022 ) . Data-centric methods instead augment or reweight fixed datasets by generating samples from adversarial environments ( Rigter et al., 2022 ; Bhardwaj et al., 2023 ) , mixing diffusion-generated synthetic data with real data ( Lu et al., 2023 ) , or downweighting corrupted samples ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . In particular, generative-model methods, as a data-centric subfamily, learn dynamics models from offline data and generates plausible future transitions or multi-step trajectories for robust policy learning ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Berdica et al., 2024 ; Foffano et al., 2026 ) . Furthermore, robust safe RL extends robust policy learning to jointly maintain task performance and satisfy cost constraints under uncertainty ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Queeney and Benosman, 2023 ) . In this work, RobustRLlib integrates 17 representative algorithms spanning robust online, offline, and safe RL, systematically organizes them by algorithm features, and evaluates them across diverse shift sources and modes under a unified protocol. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms. Related RL benchmarks. Existing RL benchmarks can be broadly categorized into data-oriented benchmarks , which primarily provide fixed datasets for algorithm development ( Fu et al., 2020 ; Gulcehre et al., 2020 ; Qin et al., 2022 ) ; task-oriented benchmarks , which offer standardized tasks and environments for developing and evaluating RL algorithms, ranging from continuous control to advanced robotics ( Duan et al., 2016 ; Yu et al., 2020a ; Sferrazza et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2023 ; Pumacay et al., 2024 ) ; and algorithm-oriented libraries and benchmarks , which provide reproducible implementations, training infrastructure, and pipelines for existing RL algorithms, serving as a foundation for downstream applications, fair comparisons, and further algorithm development ( Liang et al., 2018 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Raffin et al., 2021 ; Huang et al., 2022 ; Weng et al., 2022 ) . In particular, for robust RL, closely related task-oriented benchmarks include RRLS, which focuses on continuous control ( Zouitine et al., 2024 ) , and Robust-Gymnasium, which covers a broader range of control and robotics tasks ( Gu et al., 2025 ) . Complementing these efforts, this work introduces RobustRLlib , the first unified algorithm-oriented library and benchmark for robust RL. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms, while enabling easy comparisons with existing methods. In addition, RobustRLlib extends the considered deployment shifts to include latency and semantic shifts, and expands evaluation to advanced high-dimensional robotic tasks. There exist other benchmarks that address related settings, such as off-dynamics transfer, real-world operating stressors, and adversarial robustness ( Lyu et al., 2024 ; Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020 ; Mohan et al., 2026 ) . Sim-to-real gap in robotics. The sim-to-real gap is a longstanding challenge in robotics, where mismatches between simulation and real-world hardware can substantially degrade the performance of policies trained in simulation. Prior work addresses this gap through various approaches, including dynamics randomization ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Andrychowicz et al., 2020 ) , actuator and latency modeling ( Tan et al., 2018 ) , and online adaptation to changing dynamics ( Kumar et al., 2021 ) . These considerations have been explored in whole-body humanoid control ( Gu et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ) , safety-critical robotics ( As et al., 2026 ) , real-time VLA policies that overlap execution and inference ( Black et al., 2026 ) , and demonstration-driven policies for contact-rich manipulation ( Sharma et al., 2026 ) . However, many existing approaches are task-specific and address particular sources of sim-to-real mismatch. In this work, we provide a unified robust RL algorithm library with 17 representative algorithms covering diverse tasks and sim-to-real gaps. These algorithms and their underlying design principles have the potential to support broader robotics applications while reducing manual iteration before hardware deployment. 3 RobustRLlib : An Algorithm-Centric Robust RL Benchmark RobustRLlib is organized around algorithm attribution : it records how a robust RL method changes learning, which shift the method claims to address, and which base algorithm realizes the method. The disruptor toolbox then instantiates the claimed target shift independently of the base learner, while the evaluation platform measures both common robustness and method-specific specialization. This separation makes each result traceable to an algorithmic feature and an evaluation condition rather than treating robust RL as a single undifferentiated class. Markov decision processes (MDP). We consider a finite-horizon MDP ℳ 0 = ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , T , P 0 , r 0 ) \mathcal{M}_{0}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,P_{0},r_{0}) , where 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and 𝒜 \mathcal{A} are the state and action spaces, T T is the horizon, and P 0 P_{0} and r 0 r_{0} denote the nominal transition kernel and reward function. At time t t , the policy selects a t ∼ π t ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) a_{t}\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid s_{t}) , receives reward r 0 , t ​ ( s t , a t ) r_{0,t}(s_{t},a_{t}) , and the environment transitions according to s t + 1 ∼ P 0 , t ( ⋅ ∣ s t , a t ) s_{t+1}\sim P_{0,t}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}) . Classical robust MDPs replace the nominal transition model P 0 P_{0} with a shift set 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and seek a policy with high worst-case return ( Iyengar, 2005 ; Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005 ) : max ⁡ inf P ∈ 𝒫 π ⁡ J ⁡ ( π , P , r 0 ) , J ⁡ ( π , P , r 0 ) = 𝔼 π , P ​ [ ∑ t = 1 T r 0 , t ​ ( s t , a t ) ] . \max_{\pi}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}J(\pi;P,r_{0}),\qquad J(\pi;P,r_{0})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi,P}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{0,t}(s_{t},a_{t})\right]. (1) For safety-constrained tasks, we augment the MDP with a cost function c = { c t } t = 1 T c=\{c_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} and a budget d d , requiring 𝔼 π , P ​ [ ∑ t = 1 T c t ​ ( s t , a t ) ] ≤ d \mathbb{E}_{\pi,P}[\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(s_{t},a_{t})]\leq d in addition to maximizing task return. This cost interface is retained when shift is introduced, allowing robustness and safety to be evaluated jointly. 3.1 Robust RL algorithm library construction Problem Algorithm feature Method Target Base Shifted-env Adversarial Learned shift algorithm rollout network model Robust Offline Learner-centric RFQI Dynamic FQI RORL Observation SAC ATLA Observation IQL ✓ RSC-IQL Semantics IQL ✓ Data-centric RAMBO Dynamic SAC ✓ ✓ Generative model ROMB Dynamic IQL ✓ ✓ FWM Dynamic IQL ✓ PLR-PVL Dynamic IQL ✓ Robust Online Learner-centric ATLA Observation PPO ✓ ATLA-SA Observation PPO ✓ RSC Semantic SAC ✓ Environment-centric RARL Dynamic PPO / TRPO ✓ ✓ DR Dynamic SAC / PPO ✓ Robust Safe Robust safe RAMU Dynamic PPO SPiDR Dynamic PPO ✓ ✓ Table 1 : Structural comparison of the robust methods in the library. Online methods are grouped as learner-centric or environment-centric, offline methods as learner-centric or data-centric; generative model is a data-centric subfamily, and robust safe methods form a separate family. Shifted-env rollout marks rollouts collected from a deliberately perturbed physical environment. Adversarial network marks a learned adversary optimized against the policy. Learned model marks a trained next-state predictor used by the method. Target shift records the intended shift source. A checkmark denotes a present feature; a blank denotes its absence. The library has three tracks: offline RL learns from fixed data, online RL learns through continued environment interaction, and safe RL adds cost constraints, including robust-safe methods implemented here in the online setting. Within the offline and online tracks, robustness primarily enters through two routes: learner-centric methods change how experience is interpreted or optimized, while data-centric and environment-centric methods change the distribution available for learning. Table 1 summarizes each method’s feature, target shift, and base algorithm. 3.1.1 Robust offline RL algorithms Offline RL learns from a fixed dataset without environment interaction, making limited data coverage and optimistic value estimates for unsupported actions central challenges. Robust offline RL must also maintain performance under distribution shift. We therefore group its methods by how they address these challenges: learner-centric methods modify the objective or update, whereas data-centric methods reshape the training distribution, including through data augmentation or generative models. As standard RL baselines, IQL ( Kostrikov et al., 2021 ) and TD3+BC ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ) learn directly from logged transitions; MOPO ( Yu et al., 2020b ) adds model rollouts, and SynthER ( Lu et al., 2023 ) adds diffusion-generated datasets. These methods make policy learning less sensitive to uncertain transitions or perturbed observations by changing the value target or policy update. • RFQI: worst-case Bellman update. RFQI ( Panaganti et al., 2022 ) replaces the nominal fitted- Q Q target with a worst-case backup over transition ambiguity. • RORL: local policy and value smoothing. RORL ( Yang et al., 2022 ) combines pessimistic bootstrapping with smoothing around states to stabilize predictions under observation perturbations. • ATLA: observation adversary. We distinguish two primary routes. Learner-centric methods modify the policy input and learning objective while retaining the nominal physical transition law. items.raw_text: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms Xi Chen 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU Fengqi Hu 1 1 footnotemark: 1 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU Zeyu Shen 1 1 footnotemark: 1 3 3 footnotemark: 3 Affiliation: JHU Jiaying Xu 5 5 footnotemark: 5 Affiliation: UCSD Shangding Gu 6 6 footnotemark: 6 Affiliation: UC Berkeley Pan Xu 7 7 footnotemark: 7 Affiliation: Duke Anqi Liu 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: JHU Laixi Shi 4 4 footnotemark: 4 Affiliation: JHU October 23, 2026 Abstract Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib , an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms. The code and tutorial are available at https://robustrl-lib.github.io . Keywords: Robust RL, benchmark, algorithm library, distribution shift, sim-to-real transfer Figure 1 : The overview of RobustRLlib . 1 Introduction Despite remarkable advances in reinforcement learning (RL), its real-world deployment remains limited by robustness and safety concerns, particularly in high-stakes domains such as autonomous driving ( Ding et al., 2023b ) , clinical trials ( Liu et al., 2015 ) , robotics ( Li et al., 2021 ) , and semiconductor manufacturing ( Kozak et al., 2023 ) . Policies trained in idealized environments can easily fail under distribution shifts or disruptions affecting various stages of the interaction, such as observations ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Han et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2021 ; Xiong et al., 2022 ) , actions ( Huang et al., 2017 ) , or environment dynamics ( Iyengar, 2005 ; Pinto et al., 2017 ) , induced by diverse factors such as sim-to-real gaps ( Pinto et al., 2017 ) , model uncertainty ( Bertsimas et al., 2019 ) , noise, or adversarial attacks ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Klopp et al., 2017 ; Mahmood et al., 2018 ) . Robust RL therefore aims to develop policies that remain reliable under diverse types of disruptions and shifts, or their combinations in real-world scenarios ( Bertsimas et al., 2019 ; Tversky and Kahneman, 1974 ; Arthur, 1991 ) . A broad range of robust RL algorithms has shown strong performance in their specific type of disrupted application scenarios. More importantly, existing methods provide a rich set of robustness mechanisms and principles, including adversarial training ( Pinto et al., 2017 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Rigter et al., 2022 ) , dynamics randomization ( Peng et al., 2018 ) , robust value updates ( Yang et al., 2022 ; Panaganti et al., 2022 ) , and data augmentation ( Yu et al., 2020b ; Lu et al., 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ) , offering substantial promise across a far broader range of applications and shift scenarios. However, realizing this broader potential faces two fundamental barriers: algorithm reusability and systematic characterization of the capability boundary . First, existing robust RL algorithms are fragmented across separate implementations and training pipelines, lacking a unified library or interface through which practitioners can readily try and compare a broad collection of robust RL methods on a new application. Second, the empirical capability boundary of current robust RL remains unclear: for a given application and distribution shift, we lack a systematic understanding of how well existing methods perform, when they remain effective, and where they fail. This is largely because the methods are typically evaluated in distinct environments and shift scenarios, making cross-method comparison difficult and performance beyond their original settings poorly understood. To address these two gaps, we introduce RobustRLlib , an algorithm-centric robust RL benchmark that brings together (1) a robust RL method library with reusable implementations to substantially lower the barrier to applying existing methods to new problems, and (2) a comprehensive evaluation pipeline across tasks and diverse real-world shift scenarios. Complementing existing robust RL benchmarks that primarily focus on developing evaluation tasks and shift scenarios ( Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020 ; Zouitine et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) , RobustRLlib focuses on making robust RL algorithms systematically accessible, comparable, and extensible, while providing a broader evaluation framework (Comparison in Appendix A.1 ). Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • A robust RL algorithm library. We integrate existing 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms, understanding and systematically organizing them by their learning methods, intended target shifts, and base algorithms for applicators’ easy reference. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms. • An enhanced evaluation platform. Our extensible disruptor toolbox covers a broad range of distribution shifts, including MDP-element shifts in observations, actions, dynamics, and reward/cost, as well as control-loop latency and task-semantic shifts. It supports diverse shift modes, including stochastic, adversarial, and parametric perturbations with non-stationary schedules, enabling both isolated and compound-shift evaluation. The same disruptor interface further extends to massively parallel training in Isaac Lab ( Mittal et al., 2025 ) and advanced vision–language–action (VLA) robotic tasks ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . • An up-to-date capability map of robust RL algorithms. Evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations reveals that robust methods outperform standard references on average, but both groups deteriorate markedly as shifts intensify. A method’s claimed target shift does not reliably predict its empirical strengths, gains vary across tasks and shift sources, with online methods showing larger incremental effects than offline ones. By connecting diverse algorithm features to their measured strengths, this map provides guidance for designing robust RL methods for deployment shifts. 2 Related Work Robust RL problems under diverse deployment shifts. Robust RL addresses deployment shifts affecting different components and stages of the agent–environment interaction, and prior work can be categorized accordingly. Zhang et al. (2020) ; Zhang et al. (2021) ; Oikarinen et al. (2021) address observation shift , which perturbs policy inputs through sensing errors or external attacks. Tessler et al. (2019) ; Tan et al. (2020) address action shift , which perturbs or replaces executed actions. Dynamics shift , involving uncertainty in or changes to the transition kernel, is addressed either by optimizing worst-case performance over ambiguity sets ( Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005 ; Iyengar, 2005 ; Xu and Mannor, 2010 ; Wiesemann et al., 2013 ; Goyal and Grand-Clement, 2023 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Shi and Chi, 2024 ) or by introducing random or adversarial perturbations to physical parameters and external forces ( Rajeswaran et al., 2016 ; Peng et al., 2018 ; Pinto et al., 2017 ; Mankowitz et al., 2019 ) . Queeney and Benosman (2023) ; Ma et al. (2019) address reward and cost shifts through constraint-aware learning, and reward-poisoning analysis. Beyond these MDP components, Bouteiller et al. (2021) ; Peng et al. (2018) ; Tan et al. (2018) address latency shift , involving delays or irregularities in observation and action timing. Tobin et al. (2017) ; Ding et al. (2023a) address semantic shift , involving changes in appearance or task-relevant relationships among visual cues, objects, and goals. In practice, real-world scenarios may involve multiple shifts, such as changes in dynamics parameters, process noise, and observation noise ( Mandlekar et al., 2017 ) , or non-stationary shifts that evolve during deployment ( Lecarpentier and Rachelson, 2019 ) . Since robustness to one shift does not necessarily extend to others or their combinations, this motivates developing algorithms for co-occurring shifts and evaluating them under a unified framework. Robust RL algorithm taxonomy. Robust RL algorithms promote robustness through two main approaches: modifying the learning objective or algorithm ( learner-centric ) and modifying the training data distribution ( data-centric ). For robust online RL , learner-centric methods seek robust policies through optimization against an adversary ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) , worst-case robust value objectives ( Liang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2024 ) , smoothing the policy over perturbed observations ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , or causal-inspired data augmentation to handle spurious correlated shifted scenarios ( Ding et al., 2023a ) . Data-centric methods can collect trajectories by interacting with shifted environments through physical parameter randomization ( Peng et al., 2018 ) , model ensembles ( Rajeswaran et al., 2016 ; Mankowitz et al., 2019 ; Tanabe et al., 2022 ) , or by applying adversarial disturbances ( Pinto et al., 2017 ) . For robust offline RL , learner-centric methods address model uncertainty and limited data coverage through robust Bellman updates over an uncertainty set of transitions ( Panaganti et al., 2022 ; Blanchet et al., 2023 ; Panaganti et al., 2023 ) , and mitigate value overestimation by smoothness regularization over perturbed states ( Yang et al., 2022 ) . Data-centric methods instead augment or reweight fixed datasets by generating samples from adversarial environments ( Rigter et al., 2022 ; Bhardwaj et al., 2023 ) , mixing diffusion-generated synthetic data with real data ( Lu et al., 2023 ) , or downweighting corrupted samples ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . In particular, generative-model methods, as a data-centric subfamily, learn dynamics models from offline data and generates plausible future transitions or multi-step trajectories for robust policy learning ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Berdica et al., 2024 ; Foffano et al., 2026 ) . Furthermore, robust safe RL extends robust policy learning to jointly maintain task performance and satisfy cost constraints under uncertainty ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Queeney and Benosman, 2023 ) . In this work, RobustRLlib integrates 17 representative algorithms spanning robust online, offline, and safe RL, systematically organizes them by algorithm features, and evaluates them across diverse shift sources and modes under a unified protocol. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms. Related RL benchmarks. Existing RL benchmarks can be broadly categorized into data-oriented benchmarks , which primarily provide fixed datasets for algorithm development ( Fu et al., 2020 ; Gulcehre et al., 2020 ; Qin et al., 2022 ) ; task-oriented benchmarks , which offer standardized tasks and environments for developing and evaluating RL algorithms, ranging from continuous control to advanced robotics ( Duan et al., 2016 ; Yu et al., 2020a ; Sferrazza et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2023 ; Pumacay et al., 2024 ) ; and algorithm-oriented libraries and benchmarks , which provide reproducible implementations, training infrastructure, and pipelines for existing RL algorithms, serving as a foundation for downstream applications, fair comparisons, and further algorithm development ( Liang et al., 2018 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Raffin et al., 2021 ; Huang et al., 2022 ; Weng et al., 2022 ) . In particular, for robust RL, closely related task-oriented benchmarks include RRLS, which focuses on continuous control ( Zouitine et al., 2024 ) , and Robust-Gymnasium, which covers a broader range of control and robotics tasks ( Gu et al., 2025 ) . Complementing these efforts, this work introduces RobustRLlib , the first unified algorithm-oriented library and benchmark for robust RL. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and developing new robust RL algorithms, while enabling easy comparisons with existing methods. In addition, RobustRLlib extends the considered deployment shifts to include latency and semantic shifts, and expands evaluation to advanced high-dimensional robotic tasks. There exist other benchmarks that address related settings, such as off-dynamics transfer, real-world operating stressors, and adversarial robustness ( Lyu et al., 2024 ; Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020 ; Mohan et al., 2026 ) . Sim-to-real gap in robotics. The sim-to-real gap is a longstanding challenge in robotics, where mismatches between simulation and real-world hardware can substantially degrade the performance of policies trained in simulation. Prior work addresses this gap through various approaches, including dynamics randomization ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Andrychowicz et al., 2020 ) , actuator and latency modeling ( Tan et al., 2018 ) , and online adaptation to changing dynamics ( Kumar et al., 2021 ) . These considerations have been explored in whole-body humanoid control ( Gu et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ) , safety-critical robotics ( As et al., 2026 ) , real-time VLA policies that overlap execution and inference ( Black et al., 2026 ) , and demonstration-driven policies for contact-rich manipulation ( Sharma et al., 2026 ) . However, many existing approaches are task-specific and address particular sources of sim-to-real mismatch. In this work, we provide a unified robust RL algorithm library with 17 representative algorithms covering diverse tasks and sim-to-real gaps. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.32951 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026] Title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning Authors: Yijing Ke , Tianle Cai , Ruosong Wang View a PDF of the paper titled Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning, by Yijing Ke and 2 other authors View PDF Abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged. items.raw_text: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.32951 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026] Title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning Authors: Yijing Ke , Tianle Cai , Ruosong Wang View a PDF of the paper titled Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning, by Yijing Ke and 2 other authors View PDF Abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.32914 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026] Title: A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control Authors: Rahul Golder , Bimol Nath Roy , MM Faruque Hasan View a PDF of the paper titled A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control, by Rahul Golder and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) integrates domain knowledge, first-principles, and physical constraints into AI/ML models. In this work, we present a step-by-step tutorial of a modular PCML framework, KKT-HardNet, and illustrate how it could be used for hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization and model predictive control in a single platform. KKT-HardNet combines fast inference capabilities of neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of algebraic constraints through differential projection. It can handle heterogeneous data and enforce both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. The modular design supports custom neural-network backbones and user-defined projection mechanisms for PCML. To enable efficient end-to-end training, KKT-HardNet exploits implicit function theorem to backpropagate through the projection layer. This avoids computationally expensive automatic differentiation. This work also introduces an exact reduced-order Fischer-Burmeister reformulation and a primal-dual interior-point method as an alternative projection solve strategy. We also provide a diverse set of benchmarking problems for PCML in engineering applications. KKT-HardNet achieves orders of magnitude better performance in terms of both constraint satisfaction and inference time. The KKT-HardNet code and the benchmark datasets are available at this https URL . M. Faruque Hasan † † thanks: Corresponding author: hasan@tamu.edu Affiliation: Artie McFerrin Department of Chemical Engineering Affiliation: Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843-3122, USA Affiliation: Texas A&M Energy Institute, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843, USA Email: hasan@tamu.edu Abstract Physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) integrates domain knowledge, first-principles, and physical constraints into AI/ML models. In this work, we present a step-by-step tutorial of a modular PCML framework, KKT-HardNet , and illustrate how it could be used for hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization and model predictive control in a single platform. KKT-HardNet combines fast inference capabilities of neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of algebraic constraints through differential projection. It can handle heterogeneous data and enforce both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. The modular design supports custom neural-network backbones and user-defined projection mechanisms for PCML. To enable efficient end-to-end training, KKT-HardNet exploits implicit function theorem to backpropagate through the projection layer. This avoids computationally expensive automatic differentiation. This work also introduces an exact reduced-order Fischer–Burmeister reformulation and a primal–dual interior-point method as an alternative projection solve strategy. We also provide a diverse set of benchmarking problems for PCML in engineering applications. KKT-HardNet achieves orders of magnitude better performance in terms of both constraint satisfaction and inference time. The KKT-HardNet code and the benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/souls-tamu/kkt-hardnet . https://github.com/souls-tamu/kkt-hardnet pip install kkt-hardnet Keywords: Scientific Machine Learning, Hybrid Modeling, Physics Informed Neural Networks, Optimization, Process Control Contents 1 Introduction Mathematical models provide representations of real-world problems that help describe systems behavior and enable the analysis and identification of suitable solutions. However, constructing accurate mathematical models can be difficult for complex systems, particularly when the underlying phenomena and mechanisms are only partially known or computationally expensive to represent. In such cases, data-driven learning offers an attractive alternative, while existing domain knowledge can still provide valuable structure and physical consistency. Purely data-driven machine learning such as multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and deep neural networks (DNNs) can provide fast approximations, but its performance is often limited by scarce data, poor extrapolation, and the lack of guarantees that predictions remain physically meaningful. Incorporating domain knowledge, such as governing equations, conservation laws or other prior information, can reduce the effective search space and improve data efficiency, robustness, and generalization [ 1 , 2 ] . Scientific machine learning (SciML) has increasingly explored the integration of physical constraints into neural-networks (NNs). NNs are effective function approximators and have been widely used for surrogate modeling, physics-informed learning [ 3 ] , inverse design, operator learning, and optimization. However, standard neural-network training is fundamentally unconstrained, which makes the direct enforcement of physical and operational constraints challenging. Penalty-based approaches address this by augmenting the loss function with weighted constraint violations, but fixed penalty weights generally do not guarantee exact feasibility or satisfaction of the stationarity conditions of the corresponding constrained problem. This limitation has motivated the development of physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) methods. Different approaches have been proposed in literature to incorporate physics in machine learning models to some extent. These can be broadly categorized into two classes: (a) soft constrained neural networks and (b) hard constrained neural networks. Soft constrained neural networks, such as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [ 2 ] , incorporate physical constraints by penalizing physics violations through the loss function during training. Due to the simplicity and ability to incorporate differential constraints, this method and its variants have been successfully used to model fluid flow [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , biological systems [ 7 , 8 ] , heat transfer [ 4 ] , and uncertainty quantification [ 9 ] , among others, where first-principles are available. This involves balancing between the data-fidelity and the first-principle violation through weights: min 𝛉 ⁡ 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ℒ ⁡ ( F NN ​ ( 𝛉 , 𝒙 ) ) + λ R ​ R + λ p ​ L physics \min_{\boldsymbol{\uptheta}}\ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}\left(F_{\textrm{NN}}\left(\boldsymbol{\uptheta},\boldsymbol{x}\right)\right)+\lambda_{R}R+\lambda_{p}L_{\textrm{physics}} (1) where, L physics L_{\textrm{physics}} is the physics loss to penalize the violation of the known first-principles or physical constraints, and λ p \lambda_{p} is the corresponding penalty weight. Soft constrained methods minimize both the objective function (data loss) and the constraint violation (physics loss) simultaneously as an unconstrained function with pre-defined multipliers for each loss term. Thus it diverges from the concept of minimizing the Lagrangian where the multipliers are also variables of the minimization problem. To this point, soft constrained neural networks never guarantee to satisfy the physical constraints. This often leads to unreliable prediction or inference. Unlike soft constrained approaches, hard constrained neural networks aim to enforce constraints strictly by design. As modeling physical systems sometime require exact satisfaction of algebraic constraints that are highly nonlinear in nature, hard constrained methods have gained great attention in recent years in the scientific community. PCML combines the strengths of computationally efficient prediction capability of data driven neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of physical laws and high accuracy through projection, thereby providing both accurate and efficient hybrid modeling capabilities [ 10 ] . These methods aim to overcome the limitations of MLPs and PINNs. For example, systems having safety critical constraints are usually inequality constraints that are not well suited for PINNs. The methodological approaches for hard constrained neural networks can be classified into two general categories: (i) predict-and-complete and (ii) projection-based methods [ 11 ] . The predict-and-complete approaches first predict a subset of variables and completes the rest from the equality constraints [ 12 , 13 ] . An advance to this approach involves completion through explicit or implicit set of equations and then correction through internal gradient descent procedure to enforce inequalities [ 14 ] . Projection-based methods exploits optimization theory to restore feasibility. The strategy involves first predicting unconstrained variables and then projecting them to a constrained manifold. Advances in this method include strict satisfaction of linear equalities [ 15 ] , linear inequalities [ 16 , 17 ] , convex constraints [ 18 ] , nonlinear equalities and inequalities [ 10 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . In this tutorial we focus on the projection-based method to enforce general nonlinear constraints. There are several key advantages of projection based hard-constrained neural networks. First projection-based hard-constrained methods separate feasibility restoration from loss minimization. The projection layer enforces the constraints, while the neural-network backbone is trained primarily to minimize the loss, thereby reducing the burden on gradient-based learning. Second, the framework has a nested optimization structure: the inner problem projects the network output onto the feasible set, while the outer problem trains the network to minimize the fitting objective. This structure suggests potential connections to bilevel optimization that warrant further investigation. Third, the approach can extend to parametric optimization, where the active constraint set varies with the problem parameters. Through training across parameter realizations, the network can implicitly learn these active-set transitions, potentially providing useful approximations to the critical-region structure studied in multiparametric programming [ 23 ] . With this realization, one can attempt to use hard-constrained neural networks to learn parametric solutions of optimization problems [ 20 ] , where training encourages the neural network to generate predictions close to both feasible and optimal solution manifold. These predictions can therefore serve as high-quality warm starts for conventional optimization solvers, potentially reducing the number of iterations required for convergence. Hard-constrained learning also provides a promising approach for repeatedly solving parametric optimization problems at low inference cost, with applications in areas such as process control, optimal power flow, and trajectory optimization where rapid online decisions are required. In this article, we present a tutorial of PCML with efficient and modular implementation of KKT-HardNet [ 10 ] , a neural-network-based PCML framework that enforces constraint feasibility through projection. We provide a step by step tutorial to allow users on how to use the KKT-HardNet code and the framework for various process system engineering applications. Among the novel contributions, we extend the original framework with multiple projection strategies, including the reduced-order Fischer–Burmeister formulation and a primal–dual interior-point method. To enable efficient end-to-end training, gradients through the converged projection are computed using implicit differentiation instead of autodifferentiation through the full sequence of solver iterations. We further provide an open-source, modular implementation with support for sparse computations to exploit special structure in large-scale problems. Finally, for deployment scenarios dominated by single-instance predictions, we support ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation to reduce runtime overhead and enable low-latency inference. The tutorial is organised as follows: Section 2 provides a foundational description of KKT-HardNet and its components along with implementation details. With the basic idea of the PCML framework, we then demonstrate how it can be used for hybrid modeling of complex system 3 , real-time and online optimization 4 , model predictive control 5 , and PCML embedded greybox optimization 6 . Across these applications, KKT-HardNet is evaluated in terms of predictive accuracy, constraint satisfaction, and computational performance, with comparisons against existing state-of-the-art PCML approaches. 2 KKT-HardNet : A Physics Constrained Machine Learning Framework In this section we describe a projection-based PCML framework, KKT-HardNet along with brief overview of different components. The framework is provided in Figure 1 . Given an unconstrained neural-network prediction, the projection layer solves an euclidian projection problem to obtain a nearby feasible point. This architecture can retain prediction accuracy while achieving constraint violations close to machine precision. We begin with exploring neural networks and their types followed by a brief introduction to projection layer and the training algorithm. Though machine learning covers a broad variety of tools, we limit our discussion in the space of neural networks. Here, we briefly describe the different components of KKT-HardNet: a NN backbone, projection layer and the loss function. Note that, KKT-HardNet is a general framework where different architectures of neural network and projection algorithms can be integrated. M. Faruque Hasan † † thanks: Corresponding author: hasan@tamu.edu Affiliation: Artie McFerrin Department of Chemical Engineering Affiliation: Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843-3122, USA Affiliation: Texas A&M Energy Institute, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843, USA Email: hasan@tamu.edu Abstract Physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) integrates domain knowledge, first-principles, and physical constraints into AI/ML models. In this work, we present a step-by-step tutorial of a modular PCML framework, KKT-HardNet , and illustrate how it could be used for hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization and model predictive control in a single platform. KKT-HardNet combines fast inference capabilities of neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of algebraic constraints through differential projection. It can handle heterogeneous data and enforce both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. The modular design supports custom neural-network backbones and user-defined projection mechanisms for PCML. To enable efficient end-to-end training, KKT-HardNet exploits implicit function theorem to backpropagate through the projection layer. This avoids computationally expensive automatic differentiation. This work also introduces an exact reduced-order Fischer–Burmeister reformulation and a primal–dual interior-point method as an alternative projection solve strategy. We also provide a diverse set of benchmarking problems for PCML in engineering applications. KKT-HardNet achieves orders of magnitude better performance in terms of both constraint satisfaction and inference time. The KKT-HardNet code and the benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/souls-tamu/kkt-hardnet . https://github.com/souls-tamu/kkt-hardnet pip install kkt-hardnet Keywords: Scientific Machine Learning, Hybrid Modeling, Physics Informed Neural Networks, Optimization, Process Control Contents 1 Introduction Mathematical models provide representations of real-world problems that help describe systems behavior and enable the analysis and identification of suitable solutions. However, constructing accurate mathematical models can be difficult for complex systems, particularly when the underlying phenomena and mechanisms are only partially known or computationally expensive to represent. In such cases, data-driven learning offers an attractive alternative, while existing domain knowledge can still provide valuable structure and physical consistency. Purely data-driven machine learning such as multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and deep neural networks (DNNs) can provide fast approximations, but its performance is often limited by scarce data, poor extrapolation, and the lack of guarantees that predictions remain physically meaningful. Incorporating domain knowledge, such as governing equations, conservation laws or other prior information, can reduce the effective search space and improve data efficiency, robustness, and generalization [ 1 , 2 ] . Scientific machine learning (SciML) has increasingly explored the integration of physical constraints into neural-networks (NNs). NNs are effective function approximators and have been widely used for surrogate modeling, physics-informed learning [ 3 ] , inverse design, operator learning, and optimization. However, standard neural-network training is fundamentally unconstrained, which makes the direct enforcement of physical and operational constraints challenging. Penalty-based approaches address this by augmenting the loss function with weighted constraint violations, but fixed penalty weights generally do not guarantee exact feasibility or satisfaction of the stationarity conditions of the corresponding constrained problem. This limitation has motivated the development of physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) methods. Different approaches have been proposed in literature to incorporate physics in machine learning models to some extent. These can be broadly categorized into two classes: (a) soft constrained neural networks and (b) hard constrained neural networks. Soft constrained neural networks, such as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [ 2 ] , incorporate physical constraints by penalizing physics violations through the loss function during training. Due to the simplicity and ability to incorporate differential constraints, this method and its variants have been successfully used to model fluid flow [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , biological systems [ 7 , 8 ] , heat transfer [ 4 ] , and uncertainty quantification [ 9 ] , among others, where first-principles are available. This involves balancing between the data-fidelity and the first-principle violation through weights: min 𝛉 ⁡ 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ℒ ⁡ ( F NN ​ ( 𝛉 , 𝒙 ) ) + λ R ​ R + λ p ​ L physics \min_{\boldsymbol{\uptheta}}\ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}\left(F_{\textrm{NN}}\left(\boldsymbol{\uptheta},\boldsymbol{x}\right)\right)+\lambda_{R}R+\lambda_{p}L_{\textrm{physics}} (1) where, L physics L_{\textrm{physics}} is the physics loss to penalize the violation of the known first-principles or physical constraints, and λ p \lambda_{p} is the corresponding penalty weight. Soft constrained methods minimize both the objective function (data loss) and the constraint violation (physics loss) simultaneously as an unconstrained function with pre-defined multipliers for each loss term. Thus it diverges from the concept of minimizing the Lagrangian where the multipliers are also variables of the minimization problem. To this point, soft constrained neural networks never guarantee to satisfy the physical constraints. This often leads to unreliable prediction or inference. Unlike soft constrained approaches, hard constrained neural networks aim to enforce constraints strictly by design. As modeling physical systems sometime require exact satisfaction of algebraic constraints that are highly nonlinear in nature, hard constrained methods have gained great attention in recent years in the scientific community. PCML combines the strengths of computationally efficient prediction capability of data driven neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of physical laws and high accuracy through projection, thereby providing both accurate and efficient hybrid modeling capabilities [ 10 ] . These methods aim to overcome the limitations of MLPs and PINNs. For example, systems having safety critical constraints are usually inequality constraints that are not well suited for PINNs. The methodological approaches for hard constrained neural networks can be classified into two general categories: (i) predict-and-complete and (ii) projection-based methods [ 11 ] . The predict-and-complete approaches first predict a subset of variables and completes the rest from the equality constraints [ 12 , 13 ] . An advance to this approach involves completion through explicit or implicit set of equations and then correction through internal gradient descent procedure to enforce inequalities [ 14 ] . Projection-based methods exploits optimization theory to restore feasibility. The strategy involves first predicting unconstrained variables and then projecting them to a constrained manifold. Advances in this method include strict satisfaction of linear equalities [ 15 ] , linear inequalities [ 16 , 17 ] , convex constraints [ 18 ] , nonlinear equalities and inequalities [ 10 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . In this tutorial we focus on the projection-based method to enforce general nonlinear constraints. There are several key advantages of projection based hard-constrained neural networks. First projection-based hard-constrained methods separate feasibility restoration from loss minimization. The projection layer enforces the constraints, while the neural-network backbone is trained primarily to minimize the loss, thereby reducing the burden on gradient-based learning. Second, the framework has a nested optimization structure: the inner problem projects the network output onto the feasible set, while the outer problem trains the network to minimize the fitting objective. This structure suggests potential connections to bilevel optimization that warrant further investigation. Third, the approach can extend to parametric optimization, where the active constraint set varies with the problem parameters. Through training across parameter realizations, the network can implicitly learn these active-set transitions, potentially providing useful approximations to the critical-region structure studied in multiparametric programming [ 23 ] . With this realization, one can attempt to use hard-constrained neural networks to learn parametric solutions of optimization problems [ 20 ] , where training encourages the neural network to generate predictions close to both feasible and optimal solution manifold. These predictions can therefore serve as high-quality warm starts for conventional optimization solvers, potentially reducing the number of iterations required for convergence. Hard-constrained learning also provides a promising approach for repeatedly solving parametric optimization problems at low inference cost, with applications in areas such as process control, optimal power flow, and trajectory optimization where rapid online decisions are required. In this article, we present a tutorial of PCML with efficient and modular implementation of KKT-HardNet [ 10 ] , a neural-network-based PCML framework that enforces constraint feasibility through projection. We provide a step by step tutorial to allow users on how to use the KKT-HardNet code and the framework for various process system engineering applications. Among the novel contributions, we extend the original framework with multiple projection strategies, including the reduced-order Fischer–Burmeister formulation and a primal–dual interior-point method. To enable efficient end-to-end training, gradients through the converged projection are computed using implicit differentiation instead of autodifferentiation through the full sequence of solver iterations. We further provide an open-source, modular implementation with support for sparse computations to exploit special structure in large-scale problems. Finally, for deployment scenarios dominated by single-instance predictions, we support ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation to reduce runtime overhead and enable low-latency inference. The tutorial is organised as follows: Section 2 provides a foundational description of KKT-HardNet and its components along with implementation details. With the basic idea of the PCML framework, we then demonstrate how it can be used for hybrid modeling of complex system 3 , real-time and online optimization 4 , model predictive control 5 , and PCML embedded greybox optimization 6 . Across these applications, KKT-HardNet is evaluated in terms of predictive accuracy, constraint satisfaction, and computational performance, with comparisons against existing state-of-the-art PCML approaches. 2 KKT-HardNet : A Physics Constrained Machine Learning Framework In this section we describe a projection-based PCML framework, KKT-HardNet along with brief overview of different components. One way is considering the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of the problem to find a feasible solution (in some cases the optimal solution) to guarantee constraint feasibility. See Appendix B for brief details on solving the projection problem. While the efficiency of the forward projection problem is subject to the solution strategy used, efficiency of training relies on the backpropagation. Implicit function theorem can be utilized to make the training efficient with implicit backward gradient computation. With implicit differentiation, the projection algorithm may contain non-differentiable intermediate operations, provided that the converged solution admits a locally differentiable implicit representation. This substantially broadens the class of optimization algorithms that can be incorporated into the projection layer [ 30 ] . 2.3 Loss Function and Backpropagation While the projection layer ensures that the final prediction, y ~ \tilde{y} , strictly satisfies the equality and inequality constraints, we now present an updated loss function for the NN, based on y ~ \tilde{y} , so that the NN also learns the physics. The choice of ℒ \mathcal{L} depends on the learning task. For supervised surrogate modeling and parameter-estimation problems, the loss typically measures the discrepancy between the model prediction and the available target data. For optimization and control applications, the physical or economic objective of the underlying optimization problem can instead be used directly as the training loss. Training, therefore, consists of determining the network parameters 𝜽 \boldsymbol{\theta} that minimize the selected task-specific objective while accounting for regularization. It computes the gradient of the total loss with respect to the NN parameters through chain rule and utilizes the gradient to update the parameters. While backpropagation is efficient in gradient computation, second order methods such as Gauss-Newton [ 33 ] , Levenberg-Marquardt [ 34 , 35 ] algorithms have also shown promise to train NNs. 2.4 A Modular Python Package (pip install kkt-hardnet) Figure 4: Modular organization of KKT-HardNet . items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.32910 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026] Title: Recommender regret for improving regularised RL estimation with bandits and MCTS Authors: Danilo Vucetic , Alexandre Larouche , Mohammad Pedramfar , Audrey Durand , Gauthier Gidel View a PDF of the paper titled Recommender regret for improving regularised RL estimation with bandits and MCTS, by Danilo Vucetic and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms rely on estimators, like Monte Carlo tree search or one-step look-ahead, to provide policy, value, or Q-value estimates in training and inference. However, existing bandit-based estimation frameworks evaluate sampling efficiency, not the quality of estimates. We address this by formalising estimate generation as a recommendation process, treating bandit-based sampling as an improvement operator. To evaluate the quality of a recommendation (estimate), we define regulariser-aware recommender regrets, analysing their lower bounds, and proving that simple algorithms like uniform sampling can achieve these bounds. Finally, we unify bandit- and search-based target improvement under recommender MCTS. Across synthetic trees, arcade games, and scientific discovery tasks, recommenders often yield faster target convergence and superior downstream performance. Our experiments characterise for the first time the potential of regularised MCTS in scientific applications. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.32919 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026] Title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements Authors: Xinrui Li , Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi , Siddharth Bhat , Rianna Jamdar , Yongxi Lin , Stella Biderman View a PDF of the paper titled SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements, by Xinrui Li and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. items.content: SemantEq : Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements Xinrui Li 1,2 Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi 1 Siddharth Bhat 1,3,4 Rianna Jamdar 1 Yongxi Lin 1,2 Stella Biderman 1 1 EleutherAI 2 Carnegie Mellon University 3 University of Cambridge 4 XTX Markets Abstract Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. P ↔ Q P\leftrightarrow Q holds trivially for any two statements P P and Q Q that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through P ↔ True ↔ Q P\leftrightarrow\mathrm{True}\leftrightarrow Q . The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq , a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library’s own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval , a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq +, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq 1 Introduction Formal theorem proving has improved quickly on benchmarks such as miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench ( Zheng et al., 2022 ; Azerbayev et al., 2023 ; Tsoukalas et al., 2024 ) , in part because the Lean kernel checks every proof and gives models a reliable signal ( de Moura & Ullrich, 2021 ) . Models now also formalize at scale, from large problem sets ( Ying et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) to whole textbooks and research papers ( Rammal et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and the Formal Conjectures project collects Lean statements of open problems ( The Formal Conjectures Authors, 2025 ) . The kernel, however, checks a proof only against its formal statement, not whether the statement says what the source says. Audits of benchmarks find statements that drop hypotheses, change domains, or become vacuous ( Ospanov et al., 2025 ; Ammanamanchi et al., 2026 ) , and an expert review of an agent’s formalization found it weakest at choosing definitions, not at filling in proofs ( Ilin & Nugent, 2026 ) . As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement. At this scale no one can read every statement, so an automatic evaluator decides which formalizations count as correct. It is also often the reward for training the next formalizer ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) or the filter that keeps its outputs ( Peng et al., 2026 ) . A formalizer trained against an evaluator that accepts unfaithful statements therefore learns to produce them, and one trained against an evaluator that rejects valid rewordings is held back. The ideal evaluator would compare a formal statement with its informal source directly, and learned judges try to ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2026 ; Rammal et al., 2026 ) , but their verdicts come with no proof that anyone can check. We work in the setting where a trusted formal reference exists, as it does when large projects formalize the statements of their main results before the proofs ( van Doorn et al., 2023 ; Tao, 2023 ; Commelin & Topaz, 2024 ) and when benchmarks ship references checked by people. The task is still hard, because one informal statement has many correct formalizations, which differ in variable names, hypothesis order, library definitions, or the form of the conclusion. Text similarity to the reference, such as BLEU ( Papineni et al., 2002 ) , therefore cannot tell a rewording from a different claim ( Azerbayev et al., 2023 ) . The same problem arises across language model evaluation. Biderman et al. (2024) call it “the Key Problem”: many syntactically different outputs express the same content, and the best available tools for detecting semantic equivalence are language models, which are the systems being evaluated. Responses fall into three groups: restricting the answer space so a program can check it, grading with a model, and grading by people. Formal mathematics seems to belong to the first group, because the kernel checks proofs. The kernel does not check statements, however, so statement autoformalization brings the Key Problem back. A natural test is to prove that the candidate and the reference imply each other, but the test proves too much. In Lean, Nat.Prime 5 and Irrational (Real.sqrt 2) are logically equivalent, because Mathlib proves both. Each implication can then ignore its antecedent, the statement it assumes, and prove its conclusion outright. A candidate that states something true but different from the reference passes the same way, and a stronger prover finds such proofs for more pairs. The existing evaluators BEq and BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ restrict how the proof is found and check the proof text for the antecedent’s name ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Poiroux et al., 2025 ) . A restricted search can still close a goal from library facts alone, however, and a name in the text does not show that the antecedent did any work (Section 2 ). The question is therefore which proofs to accept. SemantEq answers that question before any prover runs. It relates two statements when each turns into the other by a chain of four kinds of step, namely logical rearrangement, rewriting with an equation or biconditional that the library states, a change of variables, and structural weakening (Figure 1 ). Our programs read the proof term that Lean checks, not the tactic script that produced it, to see which steps a proof takes and whether it depends on the other statement. Because the rule is fixed apart from the prover, it separates the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance. Any prover can search for chains, and a stronger prover can find more of them without changing what an acceptance means. We study two ways to find chains. SemantEq-Eval is a deterministic Lean metaprogram that searches for a chain in each direction and audits the proof term it finds, with no model and no GPU, in a median of two seconds per pair (mean 30.5 s, on the 407 equivalent pairs of Section 3.3 ) on a laptop CPU. On the ProofNetVerif test split, under our adjudicated labels, it accepts no non-equivalent pair, for a precision of 100% against 95.8% for BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ , and its recall is 65.6% against 61.8%. The published labels give the same ranking. On 100 non-equivalent pairs assembled to test each audit, it accepts none, while BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ accepts 54 (Section 3 ). More search barely helps. Across our grid an 8.9-fold increase in CPU time adds at most three pairs, because many of the missed pairs need a step that the search is not built to take, such as building a new object to plug into the other statement (Section 3.3 ). The second way lets a language model write the proofs. A compiling proof establishes the implication but not, by itself, that the two statements say the same thing, since under prompts that ask only for a compiling proof the model proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit reads each proof term and accepts a direction only when it is built from the four kinds of defined step, apart from exceptions it records, and it names the rule that a rejected proof breaks. It accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs and certifies 330 of the 407 equivalent pairs under the best of four prompts, against 266 for the search (Sections 4.1 and 4.2 ). Our contributions are as follows. • We define SemantEq , a relation that fixes the allowed steps by their effect, and prove that it is an equivalence relation whose related pairs are logically equivalent (Section 2.1 ). • We build SemantEq-Eval , a search without a model that improves on BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ in precision and recall, and find where more search stops helping (Sections 2.2 and 3 ). • We introduce SemantEq-ProofAudit , which audits proofs from any prover and separates equivalent from non-equivalent pairs where compilation does not (Section 4 ). SemantEq checks agreement with a formal reference, not with the informal source, so a candidate that copies a mistake in the reference still passes. A rejection means only that no proof passed the search and its audits, not that the two statements differ. 2 Better Semantic Equivalence for Mathematical Statements A good notion of mathematical equivalence should accept different formulations of the same claim. Definitional equality, which Lean checks by computing and unfolding definitions, is too strict. It identifies 1 + 1 = 2 1+1=2 with 2 = 2 2=2 but not x + y = z x+y=z with y + x = z y+x=z . Unrestricted provable equivalence is too loose, as the introduction shows. BEq and BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ aim for a test between the two by restricting the proofs in both directions. BEq ( Liu et al., 2025b ) defines equivalence as converting each statement into the other by restricted transformations, which reduce to definitional equality when none are allowed. To check one direction, it assumes the other statement, the antecedent, as a theorem closed with sorry , Lean’s placeholder for a missing proof. It then looks for a proof of the goal, first with exact? , which searches the library and the hypotheses for a lemma that closes it, and then with a language model limited to eleven tactics, Lean’s proof commands. BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ ( Poiroux et al., 2025 ) replaces the model with fixed strategies that use the antecedent through apply , convert , or have and finish with tactics such as simp_all_arith! , so it is deterministic and runs on a CPU. Both look for the antecedent’s name in the proof, although BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ does so only for its first exact? attempt and inserts the name itself in its other strategies. Appendix E shows two ways this fails on pairs that ProofNetVerif labels not equivalent. First, a closing tactic can prove the goal from the library alone. In the first pair each statement has its own direct proof, so accepting both directions says nothing about whether they state the same claim. The BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ authors report related false acceptances and a fix that is now their default ( Poiroux et al., 2025 , Appendix A.6.1) . Second, a name in a script does not show that the antecedent did any work. In one direction of the second pair the antecedent never appears in the proof term, and in the other it appears but is not needed. An evaluator therefore has to check how a proof uses the antecedent and the library. SemantEq does this by defining the allowed steps first, as BEq does, and by examining the proof term, the proof object that Lean’s kernel checks. 2.1 SemantEq : An Equivalence Relation Defined by Allowed Steps Our key idea is to fix a set of allowed steps, each simple enough for a person or a program to audit, and to call two statements equivalent when a chain of such steps leads from each to the other. We first fix notation and then define four kinds of step by their effect on a statement. Setting. Fix the library ℒ \mathcal{L} , for us Lean with Mathlib. A statement is a proposition over ℒ \mathcal{L} with no free variables, taken up to renaming of bound variables and definitional unfolding, and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is the class of statements.
