items.raw_text: SemantEq : Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements Xinrui Li 1,2 Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi 1 Siddharth Bhat 1,3,4 Rianna Jamdar 1 Yongxi Lin 1,2 Stella Biderman 1 1 EleutherAI 2 Carnegie Mellon University 3 University of Cambridge 4 XTX Markets Abstract Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. P ↔ Q P\leftrightarrow Q holds trivially for any two statements P P and Q Q that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through P ↔ True ↔ Q P\leftrightarrow\mathrm{True}\leftrightarrow Q . The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq , a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library’s own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval , a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq +, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq 1 Introduction Formal theorem proving has improved quickly on benchmarks such as miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench ( Zheng et al., 2022 ; Azerbayev et al., 2023 ; Tsoukalas et al., 2024 ) , in part because the Lean kernel checks every proof and gives models a reliable signal ( de Moura & Ullrich, 2021 ) . Models now also formalize at scale, from large problem sets ( Ying et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) to whole textbooks and research papers ( Rammal et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and the Formal Conjectures project collects Lean statements of open problems ( The Formal Conjectures Authors, 2025 ) . The kernel, however, checks a proof only against its formal statement, not whether the statement says what the source says. Audits of benchmarks find statements that drop hypotheses, change domains, or become vacuous ( Ospanov et al., 2025 ; Ammanamanchi et al., 2026 ) , and an expert review of an agent’s formalization found it weakest at choosing definitions, not at filling in proofs ( Ilin & Nugent, 2026 ) . As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement. At this scale no one can read every statement, so an automatic evaluator decides which formalizations count as correct. It is also often the reward for training the next formalizer ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) or the filter that keeps its outputs ( Peng et al., 2026 ) . A formalizer trained against an evaluator that accepts unfaithful statements therefore learns to produce them, and one trained against an evaluator that rejects valid rewordings is held back. The ideal evaluator would compare a formal statement with its informal source directly, and learned judges try to ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2026 ; Rammal et al., 2026 ) , but their verdicts come with no proof that anyone can check. We work in the setting where a trusted formal reference exists, as it does when large projects formalize the statements of their main results before the proofs ( van Doorn et al., 2023 ; Tao, 2023 ; Commelin & Topaz, 2024 ) and when benchmarks ship references checked by people. The task is still hard, because one informal statement has many correct formalizations, which differ in variable names, hypothesis order, library definitions, or the form of the conclusion. Text similarity to the reference, such as BLEU ( Papineni et al., 2002 ) , therefore cannot tell a rewording from a different claim ( Azerbayev et al., 2023 ) . The same problem arises across language model evaluation. Biderman et al. (2024) call it “the Key Problem”: many syntactically different outputs express the same content, and the best available tools for detecting semantic equivalence are language models, which are the systems being evaluated. Responses fall into three groups: restricting the answer space so a program can check it, grading with a model, and grading by people. Formal mathematics seems to belong to the first group, because the kernel checks proofs. The kernel does not check statements, however, so statement autoformalization brings the Key Problem back. A natural test is to prove that the candidate and the reference imply each other, but the test proves too much. In Lean, Nat.Prime 5 and Irrational (Real.sqrt 2) are logically equivalent, because Mathlib proves both. Each implication can then ignore its antecedent, the statement it assumes, and prove its conclusion outright. A candidate that states something true but different from the reference passes the same way, and a stronger prover finds such proofs for more pairs. The existing evaluators BEq and BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ restrict how the proof is found and check the proof text for the antecedent’s name ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Poiroux et al., 2025 ) . A restricted search can still close a goal from library facts alone, however, and a name in the text does not show that the antecedent did any work (Section 2 ). The question is therefore which proofs to accept. SemantEq answers that question before any prover runs. It relates two statements when each turns into the other by a chain of four kinds of step, namely logical rearrangement, rewriting with an equation or biconditional that the library states, a change of variables, and structural weakening (Figure 1 ). Our programs read the proof term that Lean checks, not the tactic script that produced it, to see which steps a proof takes and whether it depends on the other statement. Because the rule is fixed apart from the prover, it separates the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance. Any prover can search for chains, and a stronger prover can find more of them without changing what an acceptance means. We study two ways to find chains. SemantEq-Eval is a deterministic Lean metaprogram that searches for a chain in each direction and audits the proof term it finds, with no model and no GPU, in a median of two seconds per pair (mean 30.5 s, on the 407 equivalent pairs of Section 3.3 ) on a laptop CPU. On the ProofNetVerif test split, under our adjudicated labels, it accepts no non-equivalent pair, for a precision of 100% against 95.8% for BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ , and its recall is 65.6% against 61.8%. The published labels give the same ranking. On 100 non-equivalent pairs assembled to test each audit, it accepts none, while BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ accepts 54 (Section 3 ). More search barely helps. Across our grid an 8.9-fold increase in CPU time adds at most three pairs, because many of the missed pairs need a step that the search is not built to take, such as building a new object to plug into the other statement (Section 3.3 ). The second way lets a language model write the proofs. A compiling proof establishes the implication but not, by itself, that the two statements say the same thing, since under prompts that ask only for a compiling proof the model proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit reads each proof term and accepts a direction only when it is built from the four kinds of defined step, apart from exceptions it records, and it names the rule that a rejected proof breaks. It accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs and certifies 330 of the 407 equivalent pairs under the best of four prompts, against 266 for the search (Sections 4.1 and 4.2 ). SemantEq checks agreement with a formal reference, not with the informal source, so a candidate that copies a mistake in the reference still passes. A rejection means only that no proof passed the search and its audits, not that the two statements differ. 2 Better Semantic Equivalence for Mathematical Statements A good notion of mathematical equivalence should accept different formulations of the same claim. Definitional equality, which Lean checks by computing and unfolding definitions, is too strict. It identifies 1 + 1 = 2 1+1=2 with 2 = 2 2=2 but not x + y = z x+y=z with y + x = z y+x=z . Unrestricted provable equivalence is too loose, as the introduction shows. BEq and BEq + \texttt{BEq}+ aim for a test between the two by restricting the proofs in both directions. To check one direction, it assumes the other statement, the antecedent, as a theorem closed with sorry , Lean’s placeholder for a missing proof. It then looks for a proof of the goal, first with exact? , which searches the library and the hypotheses for a lemma that closes it, and then with a language model limited to eleven tactics, Lean’s proof commands. We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, $S^{d-1}$, to the probability simplex, $\Delta^{d-1}$. Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid $\ell_2$ gap by 97--99\% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models. items.content: 1]Mila – Québec AI Institute 2]ServiceNow Research 3]McGill University 4]Université Laval \github https://github.com/ServiceNow/retreever/tree/main/experiments/modality_gap \correspondence Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations Shubham Gupta Siva Reddy Perouz Taslakian Valentina Zantedeschi Cem Subakan Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Email: shgup1@ulaval.ca Abstract While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent modality gap . We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, S d − 1 S^{d-1} , to the probability simplex, Δ d − 1 \Delta^{d-1} . Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid ℓ 2 \ell_{2} gap by 97–99% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models. 1 Introduction Contrastive multimodal models embed diverse data streams, such as text and audio Wu et al. (2023b) ; Elizalde et al. (2023) or text and images Radford et al. (2021) ; Jia et al. (2021) , into a shared latent space. Despite objectives designed to align matched pairs, these models often converge to representations in which modality-wise embedding distributions remain systematically offset, a phenomenon known as the modality gap Liang et al. (2022) . The practical consequences of this gap remain debated. Several studies report that large modality gaps can miscalibrate cross-modal similarity, degrading retrieval and distorting zero-shot decision boundaries Zhang et al. (2023) ; Schrodi et al. (2025) . At the same time, a nonzero gap may encode modality-specific structure, and indiscriminately collapsing it can perturb within-modality geometry and harm downstream performance Liang et al. (2022) ; Ramasinghe et al. (2024) ; Schrodi et al. (2025) . Driven by this tension, a range of strategies have been proposed to manage cross-modal separation, including modifying the contrastive objective Fahim et al. (2024) , architectural fusion via shared attention layers Singh et al. (2022) ; Chen et al. (2020) , adversarial alignment with gradient reversal Sofer et al. (2025) , and alternative embeddings motivated by hierarchical structures Ramasinghe et al. (2024) ; Desai et al. (2023) . We take a geometric view of the modality gap and show that output geometry alone can close it dramatically, without modifying the pretrained backbone and with fewer than 1% trainable parameters. Our key move is to replace the default spherical embedding domain S d − 1 S^{d-1} with a simplex-constrained one, Δ d − 1 = { 𝐩 ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 d : ∑ i p i = 1 } \Delta^{d-1}=\{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}:\sum_{i}p_{i}=1\} . Although the sphere and simplex are both ( d − 1 ) (d\!-\!1) -dimensional, they encode very different symmetries. On the sphere, cosine similarity is invariant to rotations and sign flips, leaving many equivalent solutions in which modalities can match pairs while remaining distributionally separated. On the simplex, these symmetries largely vanish: embeddings are nonnegative and sum to one, forcing both modalities to allocate a shared probability budget over the same coordinates. With softmax adapters, the representation also becomes invariant to global logit shifts, providing an additional cross-modal normalization. Concretely, we freeze LAION-CLAP Elizalde et al. (2023) for audio–text and FLAVA Singh et al. (2022) for image–text, attach lightweight shared adapters, and train with an in-batch InfoNCE objective (as in DPR) van den Oord et al. (2018) ; Karpukhin et al. (2020) , changing only the scoring function: cosine similarity for Euclidean outputs versus negative Total Variation distance for simplex outputs produced by a softmax projection. To isolate the effect of geometry from architectural changes, we evaluate matched-capacity baselines. We start from frozen backbones and train lightweight Linear and MLP adapters with Euclidean outputs, and we also train Linear/MLP adapters of the same architecture whose outputs are followed by a softmax projection to the simplex. To disentangle output geometry from shared cross-attention, we use an Euclidean variant of ReTreever Gupta et al. (2026) (we call it XAttn ) that keeps the same learned-query cross-attention but outputs cosine-scored Euclidean embeddings, and compare it to ReTreever’s simplex outputs Gupta et al. (2026) . Finally, to contrast coarse-to-fine strategies across geometries, we include MRL as an Euclidean baseline Kusupati et al. (2022) with Retreever. Our contributions are as follows: (i) We propose simplex-constrained adapters for multimodal retrieval and show that they reduce the centroid ℓ 2 \ell_{2} modality gap by 97–99% across five audio–text and image–text benchmarks while matching or improving NDCG@10. (ii) We develop a geometry-adjusted gap measure, RelGap , which normalizes centroid separation by intra-modality spread, enabling fair comparison of modality gap across Euclidean and simplicial embedding domains. (iii) Using matched-capacity and matched-form baselines, we isolate the effect of output geometry and show that simplex constraints (rather than additional architectural capacity) drive gap closure. (iv) We analyze coarse-to-fine behavior and dimensional scaling, showing that Euclidean gaps grow with representation dimension whereas simplex gaps remain small across resolutions. 2 Related Work Modality gap. Liang et al. Liang et al. (2022) systematically characterized the modality gap in CLIP and connected it to geometric effects such as the cone effect and initialization-induced asymmetries. Subsequent work has refined both the diagnosis and the proposed mechanisms: Fahim et al. Fahim et al. (2024) formalize a contrastive view of the gap, Schrodi et al. Schrodi et al. (2025) relate it to information imbalance and compositional failures, and Yaras et al. Yaras et al. (2025) further links initialization and optimization dynamics to persistent separation. Empirically, the gap has been associated with miscalibrated cross-modal similarities that can hurt retrieval Ma et al. (2024) , distort zero-shot decision boundaries Zhang et al. (2023) , and hinder compositional generalization Schrodi et al. (2025) , though its impact can be regime-dependent and remains an active point of debate. Managing or reducing cross-modal separation. Prior approaches intervene either in the training objective or the architecture . On the objective side, methods modify contrastive learning to explicitly encourage alignment or reweight supervision Fahim et al. (2024) , use adversarial signals such as gradient reversal to suppress modality-specific features Sofer et al. (2025) , or propose structured/group-wise alignment strategies Grassucci et al. (2026) . On the architectural side, fusion models introduce shared cross-modal processing, e.g., shared transformer layers or attention blocks, as in UNITER Chen et al. (2020) , FLAVA Singh et al. (2022) , VATT Akbari et al. (2021) , and BLIP-2 Li et al. (2023) . A complementary line adds lightweight adapters or projection heads on top of frozen backbones (e.g., CLIP-Adapter Gao et al. (2024) and parameter-efficient tuning methods such as LoRA Houlsby et al. (2019) ; Hu et al. (2022) ), aiming to improve alignment with minimal trainable parameters. Finally, hyperbolic spaces have been explored to better capture hierarchical structure Ramasinghe et al. (2024) ; Desai et al. (2023) . Simplex and distributional representations. Simplex-valued representations naturally model nonnegative mixture weights, with roots in compositional data analysis Aitchison (1982) and topic models such as LDA Blei et al. (2003) . In deep learning, simplex/Dirichlet parameterizations appear in uncertainty modeling Sensoy et al. (2018) and in neural collapse, where late-stage features exhibit simplex-like structure Papyan et al. (2020) . Most relevant here, ReTreever uses softmax-normalized coarse-to-fine simplex embeddings for retrieval and is competitive with Euclidean multi-resolution baselines such as MRL Gupta et al. (2026) ; Kusupati et al. (2022) . 3 Method 3.1 Adapters and output domains Let f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) denote a frozen multimodal encoder (audio–text or image–text). For an input u u (text or audio/image), the encoder produces a pooled embedding 𝐡 u ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{h}_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . We attach a lightweight shared adapter g θ g_{\theta} (either linear or a 2-layer MLP) to obtain logits 𝐳 u = g θ ​ ( 𝐡 u ) \mathbf{z}_{u}=g_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}_{u}) . We study two output domains using the same adapter architecture, isolating the effect of geometry from adapter capacity. Euclidean (spherical) outputs. We form normalized embeddings 𝐞 u = 𝐳 u / ‖ 𝐳 u ‖ 2 ∈ S d − 1 \mathbf{e}_{u}=\mathbf{z}_{u}/\|\mathbf{z}_{u}\|_{2}\in S^{d-1} and score pairs with cosine similarity, s cos ​ ( u , v ) = 𝐞 u ⊤ ​ 𝐞 v s_{\mathrm{cos}}(u,v)=\mathbf{e}_{u}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{v} . Simplex-constrained outputs. We project logits to the simplex via softmax, 𝐩 u = softmax ⁡ ( 𝐳 u ) ∈ Δ d − 1 \mathbf{p}_{u}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{u})\in\Delta^{d-1} , and score pairs with a Total Variation–based score, s TV ​ ( u , v ) = − TV ⁡ ( 𝐩 u , 𝐩 v ) = − 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐩 u − 𝐩 v ‖ 1 s_{\mathrm{TV}}(u,v)\;=\;-\mathrm{TV}(\mathbf{p}_{u},\mathbf{p}_{v})\;=\;-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{p}_{u}-\mathbf{p}_{v}\|_{1} . Beyond Linear/MLP adapters, we evaluate cross-attention and multi-resolution baselines. XAttn learns 100 shared 1024-d queries that cross-attend to token-level representations and are mean-pooled into a cosine-scored Euclidean embedding, while ReTreever uses similar mechanism to produce multi-resolution simplex embeddings via softmax Gupta et al. (2026) . We also train MRL Kusupati et al. (2022) , which jointly optimizes multiple prefix slices of a single Euclidean embedding under the same retrieval objective. 3.2 Training objective We train the adapter(s) using a symmetric in-batch contrastive loss (DPR-style) Karpukhin et al. (2020) . Let a minibatch contain paired examples { ( t i , x i ) } i = 1 B \{(t_{i},x_{i})\}_{i=1}^{B} , where t t is text and x x is audio or image. Given a scoring function s ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) s(\cdot,\cdot) (cosine for Euclidean outputs, negative TV for simplex), we optimize ℒ = 1 2 ​ ( ℒ NCE t → x + ℒ NCE x → t ) \mathcal{L}=\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\mathcal{L}^{t\to x}_{\mathrm{NCE}}+\mathcal{L}^{x\to t}_{\mathrm{NCE}}\big) , where: ℒ t → x NCE = − 1 B ∑ i = 1 B log exp ⁡ ( s ⁡ ( t i , x i ) ) ∑ j = 1 B exp ⁡ ( s ⁡ ( t i , x j ) ) \mathcal{L}^{t\to x}_{\mathrm{NCE}}=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log\frac{\exp(s(t_{i},x_{i}))}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp(s(t_{i},x_{j}))} , and ℒ x → t NCE = − 1 B ∑ i = 1 B log exp ⁡ ( s ⁡ ( x i , t i ) ) ∑ j = 1 B exp ⁡ ( s ⁡ ( x i , t j ) ) \mathcal{L}^{x\to t}_{\mathrm{NCE}}=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log\frac{\exp(s(x_{i},t_{i}))}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp(s(x_{i},t_{j}))} 3.3 Sphere vs. simplex: symmetries and distance scaling Switching the output domain from the sphere to the simplex changes both (i) the invariances of the representation and (ii) the baseline behavior of distances in high dimensions. These geometric properties are important for interpreting modality gaps across domains. Symmetries and calibration. With Euclidean outputs, we normalize embeddings and use cosine similarity, so representations lie on the unit sphere S d − 1 S^{d-1} . Cosine similarity is invariant to orthogonal transformations (rotations/reflections) and sign flips, which implies a large family of equivalent solutions: matched pairs can be aligned while modality-wise distributions remain offset. With simplex outputs, embeddings are constrained to Δ d − 1 = { 𝐩 ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 d : ∑ i p i = 1 } \Delta^{d-1}=\{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}:\sum_{i}p_{i}=1\} , which removes most of this freedom by enforcing nonnegativity and unit mass. As a result, both modalities must express representations as comparable allocations of a shared probability budget over the same coordinates. When the simplex embedding is produced via 𝐩 = softmax ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) \mathbf{p}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{z}) , the representation is also invariant to global logit shifts: softmax ⁡ ( 𝐳 + c ​ 𝟏 ) = softmax ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) \mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{z}+c\mathbf{1})=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{z}) , providing an additional cross-modal normalization. Baseline distances. On S d − 1 S^{d-1} , random unit vectors become nearly orthogonal as d d increases, and pairwise distances concentrate around a constant: for 𝐱 , 𝐲 ∼ Unif ⁡ ( S d − 1 ) \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(S^{d-1}) , 𝔼 ​ ‖ 𝐱 − 𝐲 ‖ 2 2 = 2 \mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}^{2}=2 and ‖ 𝐱 − 𝐲 ‖ 2 ≈ 2 \|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}\approx\sqrt{2} in high dimension. On the simplex, typical distances depend on how dense the probability vectors are. A convenient reference model is the symmetric Dirichlet distribution 𝐩 , 𝐪 ∼ iid Dir ⁡ ( α , … , α ) \mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha,\ldots,\alpha) , for which 𝔼 ​ ‖ 𝐩 − 𝐪 ‖ 2 2 = 2 ​ ( α + 1 ) d ​ α + 1 − 2 d \mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{2(\alpha+1)}{d\alpha+1}-\frac{2}{d} . This highlights two regimes: (i) dense simplex embeddings (fixed α \alpha ) where typical distances shrink as 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / d ) \mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{d}) , and (ii) sparse embeddings ( α = c / d \alpha=c/d with d ​ α = c d\alpha=c held constant) where distances plateau at ≈ 2 / ( c + 1 ) \approx 2/(c+1) , analogous to the spherical concentration phenomenon. Estimating the regime and comparing gaps across domains. To connect this characterization to learned simplex embeddings, we estimate a concentration parameter via moment matching. Let s = 𝔼 ​ ‖ 𝐩 ‖ 2 2 s=\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{p}\|_{2}^{2} for learned 𝐩 ∈ Δ d − 1 \mathbf{p}\in\Delta^{d-1} ; then α ^ = 1 − s s ​ d − 1 . \hat{\alpha}=\frac{1-s}{sd-1}. We use α ^ \hat{\alpha} to determine whether learned simplex representations lie in a dense (contracting) or sparse (plateauing) regime as resolution/dimension increases (see § 5.3 ). Finally, because raw centroid distances can be influenced by the baseline distance scale of the embedding domain, we report a geometry-adjusted RelGap metric (Eq. 1 ) that normalizes centroid separation by intra-modality spread, enabling fairer gap comparisons between Euclidean and simplex outputs. Softmax methods consistently reduce RelGap. 3.4 Baselines Linear/MLP Adapters We use Linear and 2-layer MLP adapters in Euclidean space, and the same adapters followed by a softmax projection to the simplex. These paired baselines keep architecture fixed and isolate the effect of output geometry. Cross-attention adapters XAttn uses ReTreever’s shared cross-attention mechanism, in which a fixed set of learned queries attends over token representations, but produces Euclidean embeddings scored with cosine similarity. ReTreever uses the same cross-attention backbone but outputs simplex-valued representations via softmax and is scored with a TV-based measure Gupta et al. (2026) . Comparing XAttn to ReTreever isolates the effect of simplex output constraints from the effect of shared cross-attention. Coarse-to-fine representations MRL Kusupati et al. (2022) provides a multi-resolution Euclidean baseline (Matryoshka embeddings) enabling coarse-to-fine retrieval in Euclidean space. ReTreever provides the corresponding coarse-to-fine retrieval mechanism on the simplex Gupta et al. (2026) . We use this pairing to study how geometry affects gap scaling with effective dimension (see § 5.3 ). 4 Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate on five cross-modal retrieval benchmarks spanning audio–text and image–text alignment. For audio–text, we use Clotho Drossos et al. (2020) , AudioCaps Kim et al. (2019) , and SoundDescs Koepke et al. (2022) . For image–text, we use MS-COCO Captions Lin et al. (2014) and Flickr30k Young et al. (2014) . All datasets consist of paired items with bidirectional retrieval (text ↔ \leftrightarrow audio or text ↔ \leftrightarrow image). Backbones and adapters. For audio–text experiments we freeze LAION-CLAP Wu et al. (2023a) , and for image–text we freeze FLAVA Singh et al. (2022) . On top of each frozen backbone we evaluate seven configurations: the frozen encoder without any adapter; Linear or MLP adapters with Euclidean outputs scored by cosine similarity; Linear/MLP adapters followed by a softmax projection to the simplex and scored with a TV-based measure; XAttn (shared cross-attention with Euclidean outputs and cosine similarity); and ReTreever (shared cross-attention with multi-resolution simplex outputs) Gupta et al. (2026) . For coarse-to-fine analysis (§ 5.3 ), we additionally compare MRL Kusupati et al. (2022) (multi-resolution Euclidean) against ReTreever. All adapters are trained for 200K steps with AdamW (lr = 4 × 10 − 4 =4\times 10^{-4} ), batch size 64, and a learnable temperature τ \tau , totaling fewer than 1% trainable parameters. Metrics. We measure the modality gap using centroid ℓ 2 \ell_{2} , silhouette Rousseeuw (1987) , and a geometry-adjusted relative gap metric. Centroid ℓ 2 \ell_{2} is ‖ 𝝁 A − 𝝁 B ‖ 2 \|\bm{\mu}_{A}-\bm{\mu}_{B}\|_{2} , where 𝝁 A \bm{\mu}_{A} and 𝝁 B \bm{\mu}_{B} are modality centroids. Silhouette summarizes cluster separability via the standard per-point coefficient ( b − a ) / max ⁡ ( a , b ) (b-a)/\max(a,b) , averaged over points, where a a is the mean intra-modality distance and b b is the mean nearest-modality distance. To make gaps comparable across Euclidean and simplex outputs, we report RelGap , which normalizes centroid separation by intra-modality spread: RelGap ​ ( A , B ) = ‖ 𝝁 A − 𝝁 B ‖ 2 1 2 ​ ( 𝔼 ​ ‖ x A − 𝝁 A ‖ 2 2 + 𝔼 ​ ‖ x B − 𝝁 B ‖ 2 2 ) . \text{RelGap}(A,B)=\frac{\|\bm{\mu}_{A}-\bm{\mu}_{B}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\mathbb{E}\|x_{A}-\bm{\mu}_{A}\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|x_{B}-\bm{\mu}_{B}\|_{2}^{2}\right)}}. (1) We report retrieval quality using NDCG@10 for both directions (text → \to audio/audio → \to text or text → \to image/image → \to text). 5 Results 5.1 Simplex projection collapses the gap while preserving retrieval Tables 1 – 2 and Figure 2 summarize results across five benchmarks (audio–text and image–text). Across all datasets, switching an otherwise identical adapter from Euclidean output to a softmax projection onto the simplex collapses the modality gap by two orders of magnitude, without sacrificing retrieval. On frozen backbones, centroid ℓ 2 \ell_{2} gaps are large (0.36–0.81 across datasets). Adding a softmax to the same Linear/MLP adapter reduces centroid ℓ 2 \ell_{2} to 0.005–0.020, corresponding to a 97–99% reduction. For example, COCO drops from 0.810 (frozen) to 0.009 (MLP+Sfx), and Flickr30k drops from 0.731 (frozen) to 0.007 (MLP+Sfx). Figure 2 shows the same pattern geometrically: softmax (simplex) methods cluster at low gap while remaining competitive in average NDCG@10. Because the absolute distance scale differs across output domains, we also report RelGap (Eq. 1 ), which normalizes centroid separation by intra-modality spread. Simplex methods consistently achieve the lowest RelGap , indicating that cross-modal alignment improves beyond any uniform rescaling of distances. For instance, on SoundDescs, RelGap drops from 0.521 (frozen) to 0.179 (MLP+Sfx) and to 0.097 (ReTreever), and on AudioCaps it drops from 0.380 (frozen) to 0.180 (MLP+Sfx) and to 0.113 (ReTreever). Finally, gap reduction does not trade off with retrieval quality. On Clotho, Lin.+Sfx improves T2A NDCG@10 from 0.259 to 0.382, and on SoundDescs, ReTreever achieves the best retrieval scores (0.535/0.542) while maintaining a very small gap. Overall, simplex constraints remove modality-specific distributional offsets while preserving (and sometimes improving) the neighborhood structure relevant for retrieval. 5.2 Separating cross-attention from output geometry To separate architectural effects from output geometry, we compare Euclidean and simplex
items.raw_text: 1]Mila – Québec AI Institute 2]ServiceNow Research 3]McGill University 4]Université Laval \github https://github.com/ServiceNow/retreever/tree/main/experiments/modality_gap \correspondence Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations Shubham Gupta Siva Reddy Perouz Taslakian Valentina Zantedeschi Cem Subakan Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Email: shgup1@ulaval.ca Abstract While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent modality gap . We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, S d − 1 S^{d-1} , to the probability simplex, Δ d − 1 \Delta^{d-1} . Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid ℓ 2 \ell_{2} gap by 97–99% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models. 1 Introduction Contrastive multimodal models embed diverse data streams, such as text and audio Wu et al. (2023b) ; Elizalde et al. (2023) or text and images Radford et al. (2021) ; Jia et al. (2021) , into a shared latent space. Despite objectives designed to align matched pairs, these models often converge to representations in which modality-wise embedding distributions remain systematically offset, a phenomenon known as the modality gap Liang et al. (2022) . The practical consequences of this gap remain debated. Several studies report that large modality gaps can miscalibrate cross-modal similarity, degrading retrieval and distorting zero-shot decision boundaries Zhang et al. (2023) ; Schrodi et al. (2025) . At the same time, a nonzero gap may encode modality-specific structure, and indiscriminately collapsing it can perturb within-modality geometry and harm downstream performance Liang et al. (2022) ; Ramasinghe et al. (2024) ; Schrodi et al. (2025) . Driven by this tension, a range of strategies have been proposed to manage cross-modal separation, including modifying the contrastive objective Fahim et al. (2024) , architectural fusion via shared attention layers Singh et al. (2022) ; Chen et al. (2020) , adversarial alignment with gradient reversal Sofer et al. (2025) , and alternative embeddings motivated by hierarchical structures Ramasinghe et al. (2024) ; Desai et al. (2023) . We take a geometric view of the modality gap and show that output geometry alone can close it dramatically, without modifying the pretrained backbone and with fewer than 1% trainable parameters. Our key move is to replace the default spherical embedding domain S d − 1 S^{d-1} with a simplex-constrained one, Δ d − 1 = { 𝐩 ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 d : ∑ i p i = 1 } \Delta^{d-1}=\{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}:\sum_{i}p_{i}=1\} . Although the sphere and simplex are both ( d − 1 ) (d\!-\!1) -dimensional, they encode very different symmetries. On the sphere, cosine similarity is invariant to rotations and sign flips, leaving many equivalent solutions in which modalities can match pairs while remaining distributionally separated. On the simplex, these symmetries largely vanish: embeddings are nonnegative and sum to one, forcing both modalities to allocate a shared probability budget over the same coordinates. With softmax adapters, the representation also becomes invariant to global logit shifts, providing an additional cross-modal normalization. Concretely, we freeze LAION-CLAP Elizalde et al. (2023) for audio–text and FLAVA Singh et al. (2022) for image–text, attach lightweight shared adapters, and train with an in-batch InfoNCE objective (as in DPR) van den Oord et al. (2018) ; Karpukhin et al. (2020) , changing only the scoring function: cosine similarity for Euclidean outputs versus negative Total Variation distance for simplex outputs produced by a softmax projection. To isolate the effect of geometry from architectural changes, we evaluate matched-capacity baselines. We start from frozen backbones and train lightweight Linear and MLP adapters with Euclidean outputs, and we also train Linear/MLP adapters of the same architecture whose outputs are followed by a softmax projection to the simplex. To disentangle output geometry from shared cross-attention, we use an Euclidean variant of ReTreever Gupta et al. (2026) (we call it XAttn ) that keeps the same learned-query cross-attention but outputs cosine-scored Euclidean embeddings, and compare it to ReTreever’s simplex outputs Gupta et al. (2026) . Finally, to contrast coarse-to-fine strategies across geometries, we include MRL as an Euclidean baseline Kusupati et al. (2022) with Retreever. Our contributions are as follows: (i) We propose simplex-constrained adapters for multimodal retrieval and show that they reduce the centroid ℓ 2 \ell_{2} modality gap by 97–99% across five audio–text and image–text benchmarks while matching or improving NDCG@10. (ii) We develop a geometry-adjusted gap measure, RelGap , which normalizes centroid separation by intra-modality spread, enabling fair comparison of modality gap across Euclidean and simplicial embedding domains. (iii) Using matched-capacity and matched-form baselines, we isolate the effect of output geometry and show that simplex constraints (rather than additional architectural capacity) drive gap closure. (iv) We analyze coarse-to-fine behavior and dimensional scaling, showing that Euclidean gaps grow with representation dimension whereas simplex gaps remain small across resolutions. 2 Related Work Modality gap. Liang et al. Liang et al. (2022) systematically characterized the modality gap in CLIP and connected it to geometric effects such as the cone effect and initialization-induced asymmetries. Subsequent work has refined both the diagnosis and the proposed mechanisms: Fahim et al. Fahim et al. (2024) formalize a contrastive view of the gap, Schrodi et al. Schrodi et al. (2025) relate it to information imbalance and compositional failures, and Yaras et al. Yaras et al. (2025) further links initialization and optimization dynamics to persistent separation. Empirically, the gap has been associated with miscalibrated cross-modal similarities that can hurt retrieval Ma et al. (2024) , distort zero-shot decision boundaries Zhang et al. (2023) , and hinder compositional generalization Schrodi et al. (2025) , though its impact can be regime-dependent and remains an active point of debate. Managing or reducing cross-modal separation. Prior approaches intervene either in the training objective or the architecture . On the objective side, methods modify contrastive learning to explicitly encourage alignment or reweight supervision Fahim et al. (2024) , use adversarial signals such as gradient reversal to suppress modality-specific features Sofer et al. (2025) , or propose structured/group-wise alignment strategies Grassucci et al. (2026) . On the architectural side, fusion models introduce shared cross-modal processing, e.g., shared transformer layers or attention blocks, as in UNITER Chen et al. (2020) , FLAVA Singh et al. (2022) , VATT Akbari et al. (2021) , and BLIP-2 Li et al. (2023) . A complementary line adds lightweight adapters or projection heads on top of frozen backbones (e.g., CLIP-Adapter Gao et al. (2024) and parameter-efficient tuning methods such as LoRA Houlsby et al. (2019) ; Hu et al. (2022) ), aiming to improve alignment with minimal trainable parameters. Finally, hyperbolic spaces have been explored to better capture hierarchical structure Ramasinghe et al. (2024) ; Desai et al. (2023) . Simplex and distributional representations. Simplex-valued representations naturally model nonnegative mixture weights, with roots in compositional data analysis Aitchison (1982) and topic models such as LDA Blei et al. (2003) . In deep learning, simplex/Dirichlet parameterizations appear in uncertainty modeling Sensoy et al. (2018) and in neural collapse, where late-stage features exhibit simplex-like structure Papyan et al. (2020) . Most relevant here, ReTreever uses softmax-normalized coarse-to-fine simplex embeddings for retrieval and is competitive with Euclidean multi-resolution baselines such as MRL Gupta et al. (2026) ; Kusupati et al. (2022) . 3 Method 3.1 Adapters and output domains Let f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) denote a frozen multimodal encoder (audio–text or image–text). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.32881 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026] Title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding Authors: Nilesh Prasad Pandey , Jangseon Park , Jason Kong , Onat Gungor , Tajana Rosing View a PDF of the paper titled NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding, by Nilesh Prasad Pandey and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j, b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99x more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0x more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38x over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40x overlap ceiling. items.content: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding Nilesh Prasad Pandey Note: Both authors contributed equally to this research. email: nppandey@ucsd.edu Affiliation: University of California San Diego , La Jolla , CA , USA , Jangseon Park email: jap036@ucsd.edu Affiliation: University of California San Diego , La Jolla , CA , USA , Jason Kong email: jckong@ucsd.edu Affiliation: University of California San Diego , La Jolla , CA , USA , Onat Gungor email: onat.gungor@mail.wvu.edu Affiliation: West Virginia University , Morgantown , WV , USA and Tajana Rosing email: tajana@ucsd.edu Affiliation: University of California San Diego , La Jolla , CA , USA © none Abstract. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n n -gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes ( j , b ) (j,b) , consisting of the accepted draft length j j and target-emitted continuation token b b . A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99 × 1.99\times more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0 × 7.0\times more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38 × 1.38\times over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40 × 1.40\times overlap ceiling. Keywords: reinforcement learning, large language models, speculative decoding, n-gram caching, CPU–GPU co-design 1. Introduction Reinforcement learning post-training ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) , and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in particular ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , has become central to improving LLM reasoning ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . But it is expensive, and the cost is dominated by the rollout generation. Each GRPO step autoregressively samples many completions per prompt before any gradient is computed, and this phase alone can exceed 70% of step time ( Ji et al., 2025 ) . Accelerating rollout is therefore the most direct route to reducing the RL post-training cost. Speculative decoding ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) offers a natural solution for improving the efficiency of RL using a small drafter that proposes tokens which the target model verifies in parallel, preserving the target’s exact output distribution. However, this mechanism does not transfer cleanly to the RL rollout setting, for two reasons. First, a separate draft model or a set of trained draft heads ( Li et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2024 ) consumes GPU memory alongside the policy, optimizer states, and KV cache, and must itself be trained and maintained, an added cost precisely where memory and compute are already scarce. Second, such drafters degrade over training. As the policy drifts, a fixed drafter’s proposals are increasingly rejected ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , so acceptance falls over exactly the long horizons on which RL runs. To overcome these issues, model-free drafters ( Saxena, 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ) remove the additional memory cost by reusing tokens from the prompt or a datastore rather than predicting them, but their draft candidates are confined to a single generation, due to which acceptance stays low on the adapting traces that RL post-training produces. Our key insight is that during RL training, the rollout already contains its own drafter, for free. Because GRPO revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between steps, a prompt’s completions are highly repetitive with those generated for it earlier in training. Prior rollouts are thus a self-updating source of draft tokens requiring no extra parameters, no training, and automatically tracking the policy since they are produced by it. This repetition is especially strong for structured tasks, whose outputs are regular by construction, and it arises across rollouts of the same prompt over training, a signal that previous model-free drafters, which draw only on a single generation, cannot exploit ( Saxena, 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ) . Exploiting this signal, however, raises a systems problem. A model-free cache carries no GPU memory cost precisely because it lives on the CPU, but a naive integration then serializes the CPU lookup with the GPU forward: the GPU stalls on the host every decode step while the next draft is looked up and the step is scheduled. In our measurements this host round trip idles the GPU for nearly a third of each iteration, and the cache lookup is a negligible part of it; the synchronization and scheduling dominate. Realizing the cache’s benefit therefore requires co-designing the drafter with the rollout engine so that the host work is hidden behind the GPU, not merely making the lookup fast. To this end, we propose NgramRL, a rollout-aware per-prompt n-gram cache that acts as a model-free drafter for speculative decoding during RL post-training. For each prompt, NgramRL maintains an n-gram table built from that prompt’s prior rollouts and proposes continuations by lookup, which the policy verifies. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, overlapping GPU computation so that drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and negligible GPU time, and because it is populated by the policy’s own outputs it stays aligned with the policy rather than going stale like a fixed drafter. To keep this CPU work off the critical path, NgramRL pairs the cache with an asynchronous multipath prefetch runtime that prefetches the next step’s drafts during verification, so the decode iteration collapses to GPU busy time. We make the following contributions: • We identify and characterize prompt-conditioned temporal locality in RL rollouts. GRPO repeatedly samples the same prompts while updating the policy incrementally, previous rollouts provide high-quality drafts for future epochs. Across consecutive epochs, a prior rollout covers 48-96% of a later rollout, with recurring spans of 7-23 tokens. • We propose NgramRL, a self-updating, per-prompt n n -gram drafter constructed entirely from recent policy rollouts. Its bounded-history design limits host-memory growth and reduces mismatch with the evolving policy, while requiring no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state. • We design an adaptive fan-out prefetcher, guided by a causal budget allocator, that speculatively prepares next-step drafts for likely verification outcomes ( j , b ) (j,b) during the forward. Covered outcomes bypass the verification-dependent host round trip; uncovered requests fall back to sequential lookup without altering the target-emitted token or rollout distribution. • Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99 × 1.99\times more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0 × 7.0\times more than prompt-lookup decoding. At N = 16 N=16 , the prefetcher covers up to 99.5% of Spider outcomes and delivers up to 1.38 × 1.38\times measured rollout speedup over synchronous NgramRL. 2. Background and Related Work 2.1. Background: The Rollout Bottleneck A GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) training step consists of three stages. The policy samples a group of completions (rollouts) for each prompt, a reward model scores them, and the policy is updated from the group-relative advantages. The first stage, rollout, dominates the wall-clock cost. Completions are produced autoregressively, one token at a time, and this stage alone can exceed 70% of step time ( Ji et al., 2025 ) . Production frameworks such as verl ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) therefore delegate rollout to a dedicated inference engine ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ) . Speculative decoding is the natural way to accelerate it, but three properties of the RL setting make existing variants not well-suited for this problem. (C1) First, GPU memory is already saturated. The policy, optimizer states, gradients, and KV cache contend for device memory during training. A speculative scheme that introduces a draft model or trained draft heads adds a persistent claim on the limited GPU resource, and can incur additional GPU-side speculation cost ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . (C2) Second, the target is non-stationary. Existing speculative decoding assumes a fixed target, whereas RL updates the policy at every step. A drafter trained against one snapshot is therefore stale at the next, and its acceptance declines as the policy drifts ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . (C3) Third, rollouts are free-form yet repetitive across steps. Reasoning traces rarely have much overlap with the prompt, so drafters that copy from the current context find few matches. The repetition instead lies across training steps, where the same prompts recur, and hence single-generation drafters fail to use this characteristic. NgramRL is designed to satisfy C1–C3 at once. 2.2. Related Work Model-based speculative decoding. Speculative decoding ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) pairs a fast drafter with the target, which verifies drafted tokens in parallel while preserving the target’s output distribution. Strong methods train the drafter as a separate draft model, additional decoding heads such as Medusa ( Cai et al., 2024 ) , or feature-level draft models such as EAGLE ( Li et al., 2024 ) . The crucial difference between this literature and our work is that these drafters add trainable parameters and assume a fixed target. In RL post-training both assumptions fail, since the parameters consume scarce GPU memory and a fixed drafter cannot track a policy that changes every step. Model-free drafters. A separate line copies previously seen tokens rather than predicting them. Prompt-lookup decoding ( Saxena, 2023 ) matches n n -grams against the current prompt, REST ( He et al., 2024 ) retrieves continuations from a fixed datastore, and Token Recycling ( Luo et al., 2025 ) reuses candidates discarded during a single decode. These add no parameters, but their evidence is limited to a single generation or a static corpus, so acceptance is low on the free-form traces that RL produces. The closest work is SuffixDecoding ( Oliaro et al., 2026 ) , which caches token sequences from prior outputs in CPU-side suffix trees and performs best on structured tasks such as text-to-SQL. The crucial difference is the setting. SuffixDecoding serves a fixed model, and its repetition arises from agentic inference pipelines. We operate inside RL training, where the policy is non-stationary and the repetition arises from GRPO revisiting the same prompts. Our per-prompt cache consequently co-evolves with the policy, and acceptance strengthens as training proceeds, a behavior the fixed-target setting does not exhibit. Structured generation. The highest-value targets for RL post-training, including text-to-SQL, code generation, and tool and API calls, produce outputs with strong syntactic regularity. Completions of the same prompt share schema tokens, keywords, and boilerplate, so identical tokens recur, and copy-based drafting is known to favor such low-entropy outputs ( Oliaro et al., 2026 ) . We show that this regularity is amplified in RL training, where the same prompts are sampled repeatedly, so structured tasks benefit most from rollout-derived n n -gram caching. 3. NgramRL: Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding 3.1. Overview Figure 1 . Overview of NgramRL’s CPU-GPU model-free speculative decoding across training epochs. Two adjacent epochs show the same prompt entering GPU policy verification. A per-prompt CPU n-gram cache proposes draft tokens and receives accepted tokens to update its history. Cache contents persist into the next epoch, connecting recurring prompts to policy-aligned, model-free drafts. As shown in Figure 1 , NgramRL is a co-design of a model-free drafter with the RL rollout engine. It accelerates rollout without adding parameters, training a draft model, or claiming persistent GPU memory. The design rests on one property of RL post-training. GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between them, so a prompt’s completions repeat those it produced earlier in training. Figure 2 illustrates this phenomenon: rollouts of the same Spider ( Yu et al., 2018 ) (text-to-SQL) prompt one epoch apart share only the query skeleton early on and become verbatim identical by late training. NgramRL turns this redundancy into accepted drafts, a signal a single-generation drafter cannot utilize. Early (step 10 → \to 115, 50% shared): R1: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Companies WHERE Industry IN (’Banking’, ’Conglomerate’); R2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Companies WHERE Industry = ’Banking’ OR Industry = ’Conglomerate’; Mid (step 300 → \to 407, 81% shared): R1: SELECT billing_country, COUNT(*) as count FROM invoices GROUP BY billing_country ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 5; R2: SELECT billing_country, COUNT(*) AS num_invoices FROM invoices GROUP BY billing_country ORDER BY num_invoices DESC LIMIT 5; Late (step 1200 → \to 1305, 100% shared): R1: SELECT b.bname FROM bank b WHERE b.state = ’New York’; R2: SELECT b.bname FROM bank b WHERE b.state = ’New York’; Figure 2 . Same-prompt Spider rollouts one epoch apart (R1: earlier; R2: later). Shared spans are highlighted; overlap increases as training progresses. Three pairs of SQL rollouts from successive epochs illustrate shared text increasing with training. The early pair shares SELECT COUNT and the table and column names but differs in its predicate. The middle pair differs mainly in its count alias. The late pair is identical. Shared spans are shaded and the reported overlap is 50, 81, and 100 percent, respectively. Each prompt owns an n n -gram cache built from its prior rollouts. During rollout the cache proposes continuations by lookup and the policy verifies them exactly, preserving the output distribution. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, so drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and overlaps GPU compute. The remaining subsections detail the cache, the draft-and-verify procedure, and the CPU-GPU co-design. 3.2. Per-Prompt N-gram Cache Based on this insight, we design our proposed drafter as a set of per-prompt n n -gram look-up tables (LUTs), denoted 𝒞 p \mathcal{C}_{p} . We keep one table per prompt rather than a single shared table, because rollouts of the same prompt are more repetitive with each other than rollouts of different prompts. The cache is built and maintained in two steps as summarized in Algorithm 1 : Cache Construction: For a prompt p p , let R p ( t ) R_{p}^{(t)} be the rollouts sampled for p p at training step t t . After each step, we extract n n -grams of order n min n_{\min} to n max n_{\max} from these rollouts and insert them into the table 𝒞 p \mathcal{C}_{p} , which maps each context of n − 1 n{-}1 tokens to its observed continuation and frequency. The orders n min n_{\min} and n max n_{\max} are a design choice, trading memory vs drafting quality. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n n -gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes ( j , b ) (j,b) , consisting of the accepted draft length j j and target-emitted continuation token b b . A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99 × 1.99\times more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0 × 7.0\times more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38 × 1.38\times over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40 × 1.40\times overlap ceiling. Keywords: reinforcement learning, large language models, speculative decoding, n-gram caching, CPU–GPU co-design 1. Introduction Reinforcement learning post-training ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) , and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in particular ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , has become central to improving LLM reasoning ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . But it is expensive, and the cost is dominated by the rollout generation. Each GRPO step autoregressively samples many completions per prompt before any gradient is computed, and this phase alone can exceed 70% of step time ( Ji et al., 2025 ) . Accelerating rollout is therefore the most direct route to reducing the RL post-training cost. Speculative decoding ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) offers a natural solution for improving the efficiency of RL using a small drafter that proposes tokens which the target model verifies in parallel, preserving the target’s exact output distribution. However, this mechanism does not transfer cleanly to the RL rollout setting, for two reasons. First, a separate draft model or a set of trained draft heads ( Li et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2024 ) consumes GPU memory alongside the policy, optimizer states, and KV cache, and must itself be trained and maintained, an added cost precisely where memory and compute are already scarce. Second, such drafters degrade over training. As the policy drifts, a fixed drafter’s proposals are increasingly rejected ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , so acceptance falls over exactly the long horizons on which RL runs. To overcome these issues, model-free drafters ( Saxena, 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ) remove the additional memory cost by reusing tokens from the prompt or a datastore rather than predicting them, but their draft candidates are confined to a single generation, due to which acceptance stays low on the adapting traces that RL post-training produces. Our key insight is that during RL training, the rollout already contains its own drafter, for free. Because GRPO revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between steps, a prompt’s completions are highly repetitive with those generated for it earlier in training. Prior rollouts are thus a self-updating source of draft tokens requiring no extra parameters, no training, and automatically tracking the policy since they are produced by it. This repetition is especially strong for structured tasks, whose outputs are regular by construction, and it arises across rollouts of the same prompt over training, a signal that previous model-free drafters, which draw only on a single generation, cannot exploit ( Saxena, 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ) . Exploiting this signal, however, raises a systems problem. A model-free cache carries no GPU memory cost precisely because it lives on the CPU, but a naive integration then serializes the CPU lookup with the GPU forward: the GPU stalls on the host every decode step while the next draft is looked up and the step is scheduled. In our measurements this host round trip idles the GPU for nearly a third of each iteration, and the cache lookup is a negligible part of it; the synchronization and scheduling dominate. Realizing the cache’s benefit therefore requires co-designing the drafter with the rollout engine so that the host work is hidden behind the GPU, not merely making the lookup fast. To this end, we propose NgramRL, a rollout-aware per-prompt n-gram cache that acts as a model-free drafter for speculative decoding during RL post-training. For each prompt, NgramRL maintains an n-gram table built from that prompt’s prior rollouts and proposes continuations by lookup, which the policy verifies. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, overlapping GPU computation so that drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and negligible GPU time, and because it is populated by the policy’s own outputs it stays aligned with the policy rather than going stale like a fixed drafter. To keep this CPU work off the critical path, NgramRL pairs the cache with an asynchronous multipath prefetch runtime that prefetches the next step’s drafts during verification, so the decode iteration collapses to GPU busy time. We make the following contributions: • We identify and characterize prompt-conditioned temporal locality in RL rollouts. GRPO repeatedly samples the same prompts while updating the policy incrementally, previous rollouts provide high-quality drafts for future epochs. Across consecutive epochs, a prior rollout covers 48-96% of a later rollout, with recurring spans of 7-23 tokens. • We propose NgramRL, a self-updating, per-prompt n n -gram drafter constructed entirely from recent policy rollouts. Its bounded-history design limits host-memory growth and reduces mismatch with the evolving policy, while requiring no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state. • We design an adaptive fan-out prefetcher, guided by a causal budget allocator, that speculatively prepares next-step drafts for likely verification outcomes ( j , b ) (j,b) during the forward. Covered outcomes bypass the verification-dependent host round trip; uncovered requests fall back to sequential lookup without altering the target-emitted token or rollout distribution. • Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99 × 1.99\times more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0 × 7.0\times more than prompt-lookup decoding. At N = 16 N=16 , the prefetcher covers up to 99.5% of Spider outcomes and delivers up to 1.38 × 1.38\times measured rollout speedup over synchronous NgramRL. 2. Background and Related Work 2.1. Background: The Rollout Bottleneck A GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) training step consists of three stages. The policy samples a group of completions (rollouts) for each prompt, a reward model scores them, and the policy is updated from the group-relative advantages. The first stage, rollout, dominates the wall-clock cost. Completions are produced autoregressively, one token at a time, and this stage alone can exceed 70% of step time ( Ji et al., 2025 ) . Production frameworks such as verl ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) therefore delegate rollout to a dedicated inference engine ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ) . Speculative decoding is the natural way to accelerate it, but three properties of the RL setting make existing variants not well-suited for this problem. (C1) First, GPU memory is already saturated. The policy, optimizer states, gradients, and KV cache contend for device memory during training. A speculative scheme that introduces a draft model or trained draft heads adds a persistent claim on the limited GPU resource, and can incur additional GPU-side speculation cost ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . (C2) Second, the target is non-stationary. Existing speculative decoding assumes a fixed target, whereas RL updates the policy at every step. A drafter trained against one snapshot is therefore stale at the next, and its acceptance declines as the policy drifts ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . (C3) Third, rollouts are free-form yet repetitive across steps. Reasoning traces rarely have much overlap with the prompt, so drafters that copy from the current context find few matches. The repetition instead lies across training steps, where the same prompts recur, and hence single-generation drafters fail to use this characteristic. NgramRL is designed to satisfy C1–C3 at once. 2.2. Related Work Model-based speculative decoding. Speculative decoding ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) pairs a fast drafter with the target, which verifies drafted tokens in parallel while preserving the target’s output distribution. Strong methods train the drafter as a separate draft model, additional decoding heads such as Medusa ( Cai et al., 2024 ) , or feature-level draft models such as EAGLE ( Li et al., 2024 ) . The crucial difference between this literature and our work is that these drafters add trainable parameters and assume a fixed target. In RL post-training both assumptions fail, since the parameters consume scarce GPU memory and a fixed drafter cannot track a policy that changes every step. Model-free drafters. A separate line copies previously seen tokens rather than predicting them. Prompt-lookup decoding ( Saxena, 2023 ) matches n n -grams against the current prompt, REST ( He et al., 2024 ) retrieves continuations from a fixed datastore, and Token Recycling ( Luo et al., 2025 ) reuses candidates discarded during a single decode. These add no parameters, but their evidence is limited to a single generation or a static corpus, so acceptance is low on the free-form traces that RL produces. The closest work is SuffixDecoding ( Oliaro et al., 2026 ) , which caches token sequences from prior outputs in CPU-side suffix trees and performs best on structured tasks such as text-to-SQL. The crucial difference is the setting. SuffixDecoding serves a fixed model, and its repetition arises from agentic inference pipelines. We operate inside RL training, where the policy is non-stationary and the repetition arises from GRPO revisiting the same prompts. Our per-prompt cache consequently co-evolves with the policy, and acceptance strengthens as training proceeds, a behavior the fixed-target setting does not exhibit. Structured generation. The highest-value targets for RL post-training, including text-to-SQL, code generation, and tool and API calls, produce outputs with strong syntactic regularity. Completions of the same prompt share schema tokens, keywords, and boilerplate, so identical tokens recur, and copy-based drafting is known to favor such low-entropy outputs ( Oliaro et al., 2026 ) . We show that this regularity is amplified in RL training, where the same prompts are sampled repeatedly, so structured tasks benefit most from rollout-derived n n -gram caching. 3. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.32878 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026] Title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search Authors: Moritz Thoma , Maximilian Groezinger , Maximilian Forstenhäusler , Emad Aghajanzadeh , Manoj Rohit Vemparala , Christos Anagnostopoulos , Pierpaolo Mori , Nael Fasfous , Alexander Frickenstein , Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder , Ulf Schlichtmann View a PDF of the paper titled Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search, by Moritz Thoma and 10 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.8 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 15%.
