items.content: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search Moritz Thoma Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Germany Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Correspondence to: moritz.thoma@tum.de Maximilian Groezinger Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Maximilian Forstenhäusler Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Affiliation: University of Glasgow, United Kingdom Emad Aghajanzadeh Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Germany Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Manoj Rohit Vemparala Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Christos Anagnostopoulos Affiliation: University of Glasgow, United Kingdom Pierpaolo Mori Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Nael Fasfous Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Alexander Frickenstein Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder Affiliation: TU Wien, Austria Ulf Schlichtmann Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Germany Abstract Low-rank SVD -based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs . However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD . LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral , Qwen3 , and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.8 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 15%. Project Page & Code: https://lems-svd.github.io Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML † † affiliationnotice: Equal contribution 1 Introduction The rapid scaling of LLMs ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) has enabled previously unattainable capabilities, but introduced substantial computational and memory requirements that limit deployment in resource-constrained environments. To address these limitations, low-rank approximation using SVD has emerged as a principled and effective compression strategy ( Qinsi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025d ; Wang et al., 2025c ; Chekalina et al., 2025 ) . By decomposing dense weight matrices into smaller factors, SVD substantially reduces parameter counts and computational complexity while retaining easy-to-accelerate dense tensor computations. This ensures immediate compatibility with standard inference engines, avoiding the specialized hardware or sparse kernels that are often required by semi-structured or unstructured pruning approaches. Prior work has demonstrated that SVD -based methods yield significant inference acceleration, particularly in memory-bound regimes, while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art pruning techniques ( Qinsi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025d ) . They also demonstrate that low-rank approximation is orthogonal to quantization, allowing the two methods to be combined effectively for maximum efficiency. However, the full potential of SVD in modern LLMs is limited by two fundamental challenges: global rank allocation and decomposition quality . The primary bottleneck is the global allocation problem, which requires determining the optimal rank for each layer under a fixed parameter budget. Existing strategies fail to solve this optimization effectively, as they rely on uncalibrated local sensitivity proxies ( Azizi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) or expensive measurements ( Thoma et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) to determine layer importance. These methods typically neglect the non-linear error explosion inherent in deep networks ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , creating a critical misalignment between error proxy and actual degradation. Consequently, their ability to identify high-performance rank allocations remains limited. Further, high decomposition quality requires distinguishing and preserving the weight directions that are most critical for the downstream task. While Fisher-weighted SVD theoretically addresses this by aligning reconstruction error with the loss landscape (curvature), existing work ( Chekalina et al., 2025 ) suffers from rank deficiencies under reasonable sample counts, limiting its effectiveness. In this work, we address both challenges by introducing LEMS for global rank allocation and KFAC-SVD for robust decomposition. LEMS introduces a layer-wise error model that integrates local sensitivity, empirical calibration, and a bias correcting error propagation. By explicitly modeling layer-wise error accumulation, we can formulate the search as an ILP and solve it efficiently. KFAC-SVD mitigates the rank deficiency that limits the decomposition quality of prior Fisher-based SVD by transitioning from sequence-based to token-wise statistics for the Fisher approximation. By accumulating token-level loss curvature information, we effectively prevent rank collapse, yielding a decomposition of significantly higher fidelity. Our contributions are threefold: 1. LEMS . We propose a layer-wise error model for rank allocation in SVD that captures both local sensitivity and global error propagation modeling error propagation via a bias. To obtain global rank allocations we search the error model with an ILP formulation. 2. Robust Fisher Decomposition ( KFAC-SVD ). We leverage a token-wise Kronecker-factor estimation in SVD to mitigate the rank bottleneck of prior Fisher-based SVD and improve its decomposition quality. 3. Empirical Validation. Across Mistral , Qwen3 , and Llama 3 , KFAC-SVD improves WikiText2 perplexity by an average of 15 % over baselines. LEMS further drives substantial accuracy gains of 1.7 - 4.8 p.p. compared to the best existing rank allocation methods. Crucially, it also generalizes to activation-based SVD and scales to the 70B parameter regime, achieving a 4.0 p.p. improvement over uniform rank allocation. 2 Related Work Low Rank Decomposition. Standard SVD compression replaces a weight, 𝐖 \mathbf{W} , with a rank- r r approximation, 𝐖 r \mathbf{W}_{r} , that minimizes ∥ 𝐖 − 𝐖 r ∥ F \lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{r}\rVert_{F} . This is optimal for weight reconstruction, but often suboptimal for model performance, as deviation magnitude is a poor proxy for importance. To better match the forward computation, recent methods optimize an activation-based objective , targeting the layer-output error ∥ 𝐖𝐗 − 𝐖 r ​ 𝐗 ∥ F \lVert\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{W}_{r}\mathbf{X}\rVert_{F} . ASVD ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) weights the rows of the weight matrices by activation importance. Building on this idea, SVD-LLM ( Wang et al., 2025d ) demonstrates that whitening 𝐖 \mathbf{W} using a Cholesky factor of the input activation covariance yields the optimal rank- r r approximation for minimizing the Frobenius layer-output error. Subsequent work improves numerical stability ( Wang et al., 2025b ) and estimation accuracy of the covariance ( Thoma et al., 2025 ) while keeping the same output-reconstruction objective. Basis-Sharing ( Wang et al., 2025a ) builds on SVD-LLM but reuses low-rank bases across layers to reduce parameters on disk, creating unique memory-computation trade-offs. DOBI-SVD ( Qinsi et al., 2025 ) departs from direct weight whitening by truncating activations and fitting low-rank weights that best preserve the retained features: Because activations are modified during the forward pass, the effective objective differs slightly from SVD-LLM -style methods. It also introduces remapping, which is essentially quantization of decomposed components. BitStack ( Wang et al., 2025c ) fundamentally alters the decomposition process, separating it from prior SVD -based methods. While activation-based methods effectively preserve feature representations, complementary research targets the loss landscape directly. These methods model compression impact via a local second-order (Taylor) approximation, yielding Fisher-weighted objectives . Fisher-weighted SVD ( Hsu et al., 2022 ) uses a diagonal Fisher approximation to weight truncation by parameter importance, while GFWSVD ( Chekalina et al., 2025 ) improves curvature modeling using a Kronecker-factored Fisher, demonstrating that two-sided whitening yields the optimal rank- r r solution under this approximation. Our approach. Activation-based methods are robust but loss-agnostic, whereas Fisher-weighted compression is loss-aware. Current Fisher-based work relies on sequence-gradient fitting, sample-limited at LLM scale. To mitigate, we estimate Kronecker factors from token-wise second moments, making truncation viable and stable in large models. Searching for Ranks. Assigning different ranks to different layers can substantially improve quality at a fixed compression budget ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Thoma et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Azizi et al., 2025 ) . Existing approaches primarily differ in their search and optimization strategies. (i) Greedy rank allocation. Several methods use greedy procedures that progressively increase compression while tracking reconstruction metrics. Both MRCS ( Azizi et al., 2025 ) and FastLRD ( Luo et al., 2024 ) iteratively adjust ranks to control energy loss or weight-based similarity, aiming to keep layer-wise reconstruction error small. (ii) Balanced reconstruction error. A commonly adopted heuristic allocates compression across layers to achieve similar reconstruction errors. ASVD evaluates candidate layer-wise configurations and applies a binary search to find a uniform error threshold that satisfies a global budget. Flar-SVD ( Thoma et al., 2025 ) performs per-layer binary searches to more precisely equalize reconstruction error in vision transformers, while SVD-LLMv2 ( Wang et al., 2025b ) groups weights by type (attention vs. MLP ) and redistributes compression within each group based on relative loss contributions inferred from removed singular values. (iii) Learned rank allocation. A further class of methods learns rank importance directly. ComCat ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) introduces trainable signals for per-layer rank allocation, while ARS ( Gao et al., 2024b ) and the search component of DOBI-SVD ( Qinsi et al., 2025 ) optimize ranks via gradient-updated masks that are controlled by a small hyper-network. (iv) Further sparsity allocation. Related search problems appear in structured and semi-structured pruning. MDP ( Sun et al., 2025 ) formulates structured sparsity allocation as an ILP , enabling one-shot global optimization. ATP ( Huang et al., 2025 ) analyzes error propagation and shows that lower bounds on reconstruction error increase for later layers when early layers are compressed, motivating a simple linear allocation scheme that increases compression depth-wise. Our approach. Current rank-search methods often (i) rely on greedy updates with limited global optimality guarantees, (ii) target uniform error distributions rather than minimizing total error, or (iii) require gradient-based optimization with tuned hyper parameters. Inspired by ILP -based sparsity allocation ( Sun et al., 2025 ) and propagation analyses ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , we propose to directly minimize total error under a global budget by solving an ILP over discrete per-layer rank candidates using a layer-wise proxy model. 3 Preliminaries Current SVD -compression methods generally optimize either a task-aware importance metric or an activation-preserving reconstruction error. In Fisher-weighted SVD -compression , we seek a rank- r r approximation, 𝐖 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{W}} , for a linear layer weight, 𝐖 ∈ ℝ d out × d in \mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}} , that minimizes the compression-induced loss increase, Δ ​ ℒ \Delta\mathcal{L} . By using a second-order Taylor expansion and approximating the Hessian with the Fisher matrix, 𝐅 \mathbf{F} , ( Martens, 2020 ) we get the objective: min rank ⁡ ( 𝐖 ^ ) ≤ r ⁡ Δ ​ 𝜽 ⊤ ​ 𝐅 ​ Δ ​ 𝜽 \min_{\mathrm{rank}(\widehat{\mathbf{W}})\leq r}\;\Delta\bm{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{F}\,\Delta\bm{\theta} (1) where Δ ​ 𝜽 = vec ⁡ ( 𝐖 − 𝐖 ^ ) \Delta\bm{\theta}=\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{W}-\widehat{\mathbf{W}}) represents the vectorized change in parameters. Granularity (Shape): Solving the allocation problem requires loss estimators for all candidate ranks across weights; however, evaluating these via forward passes is computationally intractable. 2. items.raw_text: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search Moritz Thoma Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Germany Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Correspondence to: moritz.thoma@tum.de Maximilian Groezinger Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Maximilian Forstenhäusler Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Affiliation: University of Glasgow, United Kingdom Emad Aghajanzadeh Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Germany Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Manoj Rohit Vemparala Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Christos Anagnostopoulos Affiliation: University of Glasgow, United Kingdom Pierpaolo Mori Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Nael Fasfous Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Alexander Frickenstein Affiliation: BMW Group, Germany Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder Affiliation: TU Wien, Austria Ulf Schlichtmann Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Germany Abstract Low-rank SVD -based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs . However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD . LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral , Qwen3 , and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.8 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 15%. Project Page & Code: https://lems-svd.github.io Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML † † affiliationnotice: Equal contribution 1 Introduction The rapid scaling of LLMs ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) has enabled previously unattainable capabilities, but introduced substantial computational and memory requirements that limit deployment in resource-constrained environments. To address these limitations, low-rank approximation using SVD has emerged as a principled and effective compression strategy ( Qinsi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025d ; Wang et al., 2025c ; Chekalina et al., 2025 ) . By decomposing dense weight matrices into smaller factors, SVD substantially reduces parameter counts and computational complexity while retaining easy-to-accelerate dense tensor computations. This ensures immediate compatibility with standard inference engines, avoiding the specialized hardware or sparse kernels that are often required by semi-structured or unstructured pruning approaches. Prior work has demonstrated that SVD -based methods yield significant inference acceleration, particularly in memory-bound regimes, while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art pruning techniques ( Qinsi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025d ) . They also demonstrate that low-rank approximation is orthogonal to quantization, allowing the two methods to be combined effectively for maximum efficiency. However, the full potential of SVD in modern LLMs is limited by two fundamental challenges: global rank allocation and decomposition quality . The primary bottleneck is the global allocation problem, which requires determining the optimal rank for each layer under a fixed parameter budget. Existing strategies fail to solve this optimization effectively, as they rely on uncalibrated local sensitivity proxies ( Azizi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) or expensive measurements ( Thoma et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) to determine layer importance. These methods typically neglect the non-linear error explosion inherent in deep networks ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , creating a critical misalignment between error proxy and actual degradation. Consequently, their ability to identify high-performance rank allocations remains limited. Further, high decomposition quality requires distinguishing and preserving the weight directions that are most critical for the downstream task. While Fisher-weighted SVD theoretically addresses this by aligning reconstruction error with the loss landscape (curvature), existing work ( Chekalina et al., 2025 ) suffers from rank deficiencies under reasonable sample counts, limiting its effectiveness. In this work, we address both challenges by introducing LEMS for global rank allocation and KFAC-SVD for robust decomposition. LEMS introduces a layer-wise error model that integrates local sensitivity, empirical calibration, and a bias correcting error propagation. By explicitly modeling layer-wise error accumulation, we can formulate the search as an ILP and solve it efficiently. KFAC-SVD mitigates the rank deficiency that limits the decomposition quality of prior Fisher-based SVD by transitioning from sequence-based to token-wise statistics for the Fisher approximation. By accumulating token-level loss curvature information, we effectively prevent rank collapse, yielding a decomposition of significantly higher fidelity. Our contributions are threefold: 1. LEMS . We propose a layer-wise error model for rank allocation in SVD that captures both local sensitivity and global error propagation modeling error propagation via a bias. To obtain global rank allocations we search the error model with an ILP formulation. 2. Robust Fisher Decomposition ( KFAC-SVD ). We leverage a token-wise Kronecker-factor estimation in SVD to mitigate the rank bottleneck of prior Fisher-based SVD and improve its decomposition quality. 3. Empirical Validation. Across Mistral , Qwen3 , and Llama 3 , KFAC-SVD improves WikiText2 perplexity by an average of 15 % over baselines. LEMS further drives substantial accuracy gains of 1.7 - 4.8 p.p. compared to the best existing rank allocation methods. Crucially, it also generalizes to activation-based SVD and scales to the 70B parameter regime, achieving a 4.0 p.p. improvement over uniform rank allocation. 2 Related Work Low Rank Decomposition. Standard SVD compression replaces a weight, 𝐖 \mathbf{W} , with a rank- r r approximation, 𝐖 r \mathbf{W}_{r} , that minimizes ∥ 𝐖 − 𝐖 r ∥ F \lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{r}\rVert_{F} . This is optimal for weight reconstruction, but often suboptimal for model performance, as deviation magnitude is a poor proxy for importance. To better match the forward computation, recent methods optimize an activation-based objective , targeting the layer-output error ∥ 𝐖𝐗 − 𝐖 r ​ 𝐗 ∥ F \lVert\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{W}_{r}\mathbf{X}\rVert_{F} . ASVD ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) weights the rows of the weight matrices by activation importance. Building on this idea, SVD-LLM ( Wang et al., 2025d ) demonstrates that whitening 𝐖 \mathbf{W} using a Cholesky factor of the input activation covariance yields the optimal rank- r r approximation for minimizing the Frobenius layer-output error. Subsequent work improves numerical stability ( Wang et al., 2025b ) and estimation accuracy of the covariance ( Thoma et al., 2025 ) while keeping the same output-reconstruction objective. Basis-Sharing ( Wang et al., 2025a ) builds on SVD-LLM but reuses low-rank bases across layers to reduce parameters on disk, creating unique memory-computation trade-offs. DOBI-SVD ( Qinsi et al., 2025 ) departs from direct weight whitening by truncating activations and fitting low-rank weights that best preserve the retained features: Because activations are modified during the forward pass, the effective objective differs slightly from SVD-LLM -style methods. It also introduces remapping, which is essentially quantization of decomposed components. BitStack ( Wang et al., 2025c ) fundamentally alters the decomposition process, separating it from prior SVD -based methods. While activation-based methods effectively preserve feature representations, complementary research targets the loss landscape directly. These methods model compression impact via a local second-order (Taylor) approximation, yielding Fisher-weighted objectives . Fisher-weighted SVD ( Hsu et al., 2022 ) uses a diagonal Fisher approximation to weight truncation by parameter importance, while GFWSVD ( Chekalina et al., 2025 ) improves curvature modeling using a Kronecker-factored Fisher, demonstrating that two-sided whitening yields the optimal rank- r r solution under this approximation. Our approach. Activation-based methods are robust but loss-agnostic, whereas Fisher-weighted compression is loss-aware. Current Fisher-based work relies on sequence-gradient fitting, sample-limited at LLM scale. To mitigate, we estimate Kronecker factors from token-wise second moments, making truncation viable and stable in large models. Searching for Ranks. Assigning different ranks to different layers can substantially improve quality at a fixed compression budget ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Thoma et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Azizi et al., 2025 ) . Existing approaches primarily differ in their search and optimization strategies. (i) Greedy rank allocation. Several methods use greedy procedures that progressively increase compression while tracking reconstruction metrics. Both MRCS ( Azizi et al., 2025 ) and FastLRD ( Luo et al., 2024 ) iteratively adjust ranks to control energy loss or weight-based similarity, aiming to keep layer-wise reconstruction error small. (ii) Balanced reconstruction error. A commonly adopted heuristic allocates compression across layers to achieve similar reconstruction errors. ASVD evaluates candidate layer-wise configurations and applies a binary search to find a uniform error threshold that satisfies a global budget. Flar-SVD ( Thoma et al., 2025 ) performs per-layer binary searches to more precisely equalize reconstruction error in vision transformers, while SVD-LLMv2 ( Wang et al., 2025b ) groups weights by type (attention vs. MLP ) and redistributes compression within each group based on relative loss contributions inferred from removed singular values. (iii) Learned rank allocation. A further class of methods learns rank importance directly. ComCat ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) introduces trainable signals for per-layer rank allocation, while ARS ( Gao et al., 2024b ) and the search component of DOBI-SVD ( Qinsi et al., 2025 ) optimize ranks via gradient-updated masks that are controlled by a small hyper-network. (iv) Further sparsity allocation. Related search problems appear in structured and semi-structured pruning. MDP ( Sun et al., 2025 ) formulates structured sparsity allocation as an ILP , enabling one-shot global optimization. ATP ( Huang et al., 2025 ) analyzes error propagation and shows that lower bounds on reconstruction error increase for later layers when early layers are compressed, motivating a simple linear allocation scheme that increases compression depth-wise. Our approach. Current rank-search methods often (i) rely on greedy updates with limited global optimality guarantees, (ii) target uniform error distributions rather than minimizing total error, or (iii) require gradient-based optimization with tuned hyper parameters. Inspired by ILP -based sparsity allocation ( Sun et al., 2025 ) and propagation analyses ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , we propose to directly minimize total error under a global budget by solving an ILP over discrete per-layer rank candidates using a layer-wise proxy model. 3 Preliminaries Current SVD -compression methods generally optimize either a task-aware importance metric or an activation-preserving reconstruction error. In Fisher-weighted SVD -compression , we seek a rank- r r approximation, 𝐖 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{W}} , for a linear layer weight, 𝐖 ∈ ℝ d out × d in \mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}} , that minimizes the compression-induced loss increase, Δ ​ ℒ \Delta\mathcal{L} .
